# PREFACE
### BY THE
# TRANSLATOR.

JUST as the prefaces of translated works usually serve to impress upon the readers the idea that the work, upon which one has bestowed the effort of translating, is both useful and rare, and that the genius of the Author well deserved to be revealed to others beyond his own countrymen; so I see no necessity why I should dwell long on saying much of either. The utility of chronology <note>The translator uses the Dutch term *tydkunde*, literally "time-knowledge," referring to the science of arranging historical events in their proper order.</note>, for the proper understanding of ancient and modern histories, is so well known to all book-lovers that it would be like lighting a candle at high noon if I wished to demonstrate it with words. 

And this science is especially useful and necessary if its practitioners, without relying on the authority of others, forge a new path to bring the events of past centuries to their proper time based on solid grounds, and thereby spread a new light over ancient history, as the Author has done in very many places in this work. And if rarity adds anything to the value of a matter, this book shall take the prize above many others; since concerning this un- <note>The text cuts off here due to the page break; the catchword "der-" indicates the next page begins with "onderwerp" (subject).</note>

If one now examines the cited pages of the larger work regarding other places where a double date is found, one will find the years of Nabonassar <term>Era of Nabonassar</term> <note>An era beginning in 747 BC, named after the Babylonian king Nabonassar. This method of pointing out the Author’s oversights <note>original: *verzinningen*. In this context, it refers to inconsistencies or slips in Newton's calculations rather than intentional "fictions."</note>, which I judged to be the least burdensome for the Reader, led me to make two other additions to the *Short Chronicle* which are not found in the English edition: namely, the reference to the pages where each matter is discussed more extensively in the larger work, and then the column with the chronology of Nabonassar. The first was completely necessary in view of the places where there was some contradiction between the two works, unless I wanted to leave the Reader the trouble of looking everything up themselves; and, since this reference could also be useful for easily finding the proofs that the Knight <note>original: *de Ridder*. Referring to Sir Isaac Newton, who was knighted in 1705.</note> gives for each of his propositions, I have taken the trouble to do so at every place in the Chronicle.

# FROM THE TRANSLATOR.

...avoidable to show the Author’s <note>Referring to Sir Isaac Newton, the author of the work being translated.</note> views at a glance, without the reader needing to take the trouble himself to calculate the two chronologies in those places where there is some contradiction, and to keep the point where the Era of Nabonassar begins accurately in view, as everyone can see without my needing to say more about it.

With these two types of chronology—namely, the years before Christ and the *Era* <term>Era</term> <note>A system of chronology starting from a specific point in time; here referring to the 747 BC starting point of the Babylonian system.</note> of Nabonassar—I could have left it at that, as far as the nature of the matter strictly required. However, it occurred to me that it would not be out of place if the years of the age of the World were indicated for a work which is primarily intended to prove that the events of Egypt, Assyria, Greece, etc., occurred much further from the World's beginning than has been stated by the ancient chronologists; and to show from this that the World is no older than Moses relates to us; therefore, I have done so in a third column. Even if this does not serve to provide any aid to the chronology, one can at least see from it how long after the creation the arts and sciences first arrived in Europe. 

But since there is perhaps no matter about which scholars differ more than the true age of the World, I have limited myself to the proposition of the renowned Archbishop *Usher* <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), an Irish Archbishop whose influential "Ussher Chronology" placed the date of Creation at 4004 BC.</note>, who calculates the correct year of Christ's birth (which falls four years before the common reckoning, which Mr. *Newton* has also followed) as the four-thousandth since the creation. I deemed it safest, among so many differing opinions, to follow the path of so great a man in the republic of letters <note>original: *gemeenebeſt der geletterden*. This term refers to the international community of scholars and intellectuals in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note>.

### THE TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE.

This is what I deemed necessary to say regarding my additions to the *Short Chronicle* <note>Referring to the "Short Chronicle" which often accompanied Newton's larger work on ancient kingdoms.</note>. To the larger work, nothing has been added except for a list of the Scriptural texts cited therein; this was done so that one might more easily verify how the author interpreted a particular passage without having to go through the trouble of leafing through the entire book. Certain passages from the ancient authors, which the Knight <note>Sir Isaac Newton, often referred to as "the Knight" (de Ridder) in Dutch translations of the period following his knighthood in 1705.</note> had set down only in their original languages, the Dutch reader <note>original: "Nederduitsche Lezer"</note> will now also find translated here; since one of my friends, well-versed in the Latin and Greek tongues, took the trouble to translate them at my request. I do not deem it necessary to say anything regarding one or two notes at the end of the work; because the reader will easily see that these were not written by Mr. Newton. Thus I conclude this preface, with the request that the reader might kindly correct some printing errors <term>printing errors</term> <note>original: "drukfeilen." In the 18th century, manual typesetting often led to errors, especially in works heavy with dates and numbers.</note> which, due to my absence from the printers and the great multitude of dates, have crept in; all those I have been able to discover are pointed out at the end of the work.

# N O T I C E
## F R O M  T H E
# ENGLISH PUBLISHER.

*Although The Chronology of Ancient Kingdoms Amended \* <note>original: "de Tydrekening der oude Koninkryken verbetert." This refers to Newton's major work on historical timelines, published shortly after his death.</note>, had been prepared by the author over many years, he nevertheless revised his work recently, and was actually busy preparing it for the printing press when he was overtaken by death. But he never intended to publish the Short Chronicle <note>A condensed timeline that Newton originally wrote for the Princess of Wales, which was later leaked and published in France without his permission, prompting him to prepare this fuller volume.</note>, so he did not revise it as accurately. To this the reader must attribute any instances where the Short Chronicle does not precisely agree in its dates <term>dates</term> <note>original: "Jaartallen," referring to specific calendar years or chronological markers.</note> with the larger work. The sixth chapter, unlike the others, was not written out in a clean copy, leading to doubts as to whether it was Mr. Newton's intention to have it printed; but since it was found among his papers, and it clearly appeared to be a continuation of the other work—and was also summarized as such in the Short Chronicle—it was thought best to include it.*

### I N T R O D U C T I O N.

Since the Greeks, before the conquest of Asia by Cyrus the Persian <note>Cyrus the Great, who reigned c. 559–530 BCE.</note>, wrote only in verse, their antiquities are full of poetic embellishments. Around that time, *Pherecydes the Syrian* and *Cadmus of Miletus* introduced the manner of writing in prose. *Pherecydes of Athens*, who flourished at the end of the reign of Darius Hystaspes <note>Darius I of Persia, known for his conflict with the Greeks at Marathon.</note>, wrote about antiquity, arranged his chronology according to generations <term>generations: Newton often calculated history based on the average length of human lifespans or reigns, which he believed earlier historians had overestimated.</term>, or the natural reproduction of men; and was considered one of the best genealogists. *Epimenides*, the historian, kept the same order in his books: and *Hellanicus*, who wrote twelve years before *Herodotus* <note>Known as the "Father of History," writing in the 5th century BCE.</note>, calculated time by the years or successions of the Priestesses of the Argive Juno <note>Hera of Argos; using the succession of priestesses was a very early method of record-keeping before a standardized calendar existed.</note>. Others base their chronology on the years of the Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> Kings, or on those of the Archons <note>original: "Vorsten" (Princes/Leaders). In Athens, these were the chief magistrates.</note> of Athens. About thirty years before the fall of the Persian monarchy, *Hippias of Elis* published a handbook, or list, of the victors in the Olympic Games; and twenty years later, or ten years before

<summary>This introduction explains that early Greek history was recorded in verse and was thus unreliable, until later scholars began using prose and systematic lists—like those of Olympic victors or priestesses—to track time.</summary>
<keywords>Chronology, Greeks, Cyrus the Persian, Pherecydes, Herodotus, Hippias of Elis, Olympic Games, historiography</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Short Chronicle," shifting from the earliest prose writers to the historians who attempted to systematize Greek chronology after the conquests of Alexander the Great. It focuses on the transition from counting by "generations" to the more formal system of Olympiads.</meta>

## SHORT CHRONICLE.
<meta>catchword: and</meta>

After the fall of Persia, *Ephorus*, the student of *Isocrates*, compiled a chronological history of Greece, beginning with the return of the Heraclidae <note>The "Return of the Heraclidae" refers to the legendary conquest of the Peloponnese by the descendants of Hercules, traditionally marking the end of the Heroic Age.</note> into the Peloponnese, and ending with the siege of Perinthus, in the twentieth year of Philip, the father of Alexander the Great. This man calculated time by generations; for the method of calculating by the Olympic Games, or Olympiads <term>Olympiads: A four-year period used as a unit of time by the ancient Greeks, starting from the first recorded victory in the Olympic Games in 776 BCE.</term>, was not yet in use at that time; likewise, it does not appear that the years of the reigns of the Kings were recorded. The Arundel marbles <note>The Parian Chronicle, part of the Arundel Marbles collection, is a Greek inscription on marble providing a timeline of events from 1582 BCE to 264 BCE.</note> were inscribed sixty years after the death of Alexander the Great, that is, in the fourth year of the 128th Olympiad, and yet the Olympiads are not mentioned on them: but in the following Olympiad, *Timaeus of Sicily* wrote a history, in several books, up to his own lifetime, in which he followed that chronological system. In this work, he compared the times of the Spartan Ephors <note>Senior magistrates in Sparta.</note> and Kings, the Athenian Leaders and the Priestesses of Argos, with those of the victors in the Olympic games: in order to bring the Olympiads, the lives and successions of the Kings, Leaders, and Priestesses, and the poetic histories, all into agreement with one another according to his best judgment: and where he left off his work, *Polybius* began and continued the history.

It was then shortly after the death of Alexander that one began to set down the generations, reigns, and successions of the Princes in a specific number of years; but by making those reigns and successions of equal duration with the generations, and setting three generations within a hundred or a hundred and twenty years, the writers made Greek events three or four hundred years older than they truly were. And this was, however, the origin or foundation of the technical chronology of the Greeks. *Eratosthenes* wrote about a hundred years after Alexander's death: he was followed by *Apollodorus*; and these two have since been followed by all chronologists.

But how uncertain their chronology is, and how doubtful it was considered by the Greeks of that time, can be seen from these passages of *Plutarch*. "Some, <margin>[a] From the *Life of Lycurgus*, at the beginning. <note>original: "De vita Lycurgi ab initio."</note></margin> (a) he says,

It appears that the chronologists had set the time of Solon’s legislation too early to be compatible with that meeting.

To resolve such contradictions, the chronologists have sometimes doubled the persons. When the poets had thus transformed Io, the daughter of Inachus, into the Egyptian Isis, the chronologists made Osiris or Bacchus, the husband of Isis, and his mistress Ariadne as old as Io; and they feigned that there were two (c) Ariadnes, one the lover of Bacchus and the other of Theseus; likewise two Minoses, as their fathers, and a younger Io, the daughter of Jasus, which name they wrote as a corruption of Inachus. And as for the chronology of the (e) Latins <note>The early inhabitants of central Italy, including the Romans</note>, it is even more uncertain. *Plutarch* and *Servius* express great doubts regarding the origins of Rome. The ancient records of the Latins were burned by the Gauls fifty-four years before the death of Alexander the Great; and *Quintus Fabius Pictor*, the oldest Latin writer, lived only a hundred years after that Prince.

According to sacred history <note>This refers to the historical accounts found in the Bible</note>, the Assyrian monarchy began with (f) Pul and Tiglath-Pileser, and lasted about a hundred and seventy years. *Herodotus*, agreeing with this, places (g) Semiramis only five generations, or about a hundred and sixty-six years, earlier than Nitocris, the mother of the last King of Babylon. But *Ctesias* makes Semiramis 1,500 years older than Nitocris, and embellishes a (h) long series of Assyrian Kings whose names are neither native to that land nor have any kinship with the Assyrian names we find in the Holy Scriptures.

The Egyptian Priests told *Herodotus* that King Menes built the city of Memphis and the magnificent temple of Vulcan <note>original: "Vulkaan"; the Greek god Hephaestus, often identified with the Roman Vulcan</note> that stood within its walls; and that Rhampsinitius, Moeris, Asychis, and Psammitichus added splendid gates to that temple. And it is not probable that Memphis was famous before the times of *Homer*, as that poet mentions nothing of it; nor that the construction of a temple could last longer than two or three centuries. Now, the reign of Psammitichus began 655 years before Christ, and I place the start of the construction of this temple by Menes about 257 years earlier: but the Egyptian Priests had so embellished their antiquities before the time of *Herodotus* that they told him that from Menes to Moeris—the latter of whom reigned 200 years before Psammitichus—three hundred and thirty Kings had ruled in Egypt, whose reigns spanned as many centuries as...

When Joshua entered the promised land with the tribes of Israel, a <gloss>(m)</gloss> great number of the Canaanites fled before him to Egypt, where they conquered the King of Lower Egypt, named Timaus, Thamus, or Thammuz, and continued to rule in that region under their Kings Salatis, Beon, Apachnas, Apofis, Janias, Assis, and others, until the days of Eli and Samuel, who were Judges of Israel. This circle remained in existence until Cambyses <note>The Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE</note> plundered the Egyptian temples: and from this monument I conclude that Amenophis introduced the use of the solar year and established its beginning at one of the four cardinal points of the heavens. For if the beginning of it had not been determined, the rising and setting of the stars on each day of the circle could not have been recorded. The Egyptian priests then continued, during the reign of Amenophis, to observe the rising and setting of the stars every day: and when they, through the midday altitudes of the sun, had discovered the points of the solstices and equinoxes according to the common movement of the sun (for the <term>Equation</term> <note>The 'Equation of Time' refers to the difference between apparent solar time (sundial) and mean solar time (clock); this adjustment was not yet understood by early astronomers</note> of the same was not yet known), they placed <margin>(f) Page 28.</margin> the beginning of this year at the spring equinox, and founded |

This reckoning of years being subsequently brought into Chaldea <note>A region in ancient Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq)</note>, the Chaldeans <margin>(g)</margin> began their Era of Nabonassar <note>A chronological era starting in 747 BCE, famously used by the astronomer Ptolemy</note> on the same day of the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the Egyptian calendar</note> as the Egyptians, and made it of the same length as the Egyptian year. And if this year first took effect on the day after the point of the vernal equinox, then it was brought into use three or four years earlier, and here we may place the death of Amenophis <note>The Pharaoh Amenhotep, often conflated with the mythological hero Memnon</note>. The Greeks embellished the story, claiming this Prince was the son of Tithonus <note>A figure in Greek mythology, the lover of Eos, the Dawn</note>, and consequently he was born after Sesostris <note>A legendary Egyptian king said to have conquered the world</note> had returned to Egypt with Tithonus and other prisoners; and thus he could have been about 70 or 75 years old when he died. |

### CHAPTER I.
#### *Concerning the Antiquities of the Greeks.*

Before people began to record a precise chronology <note>The science of arranging events in their order of occurrence in time.</note> in history, there was a tendency among all nations to glorify their ancient origins; an inclination that was nurtured by their mutual disputes over their beginnings. <margin>(a) Book 2.</margin> *Herodotus* (a) relates that the Egyptian Priests, from the reign of Menes <note>Traditionally regarded as the first human king of Egypt and the founder of the first dynasty.</note> to that of Sethon <note>An Egyptian priest-king; according to legend, his prayers led to a swarm of field mice eating the bowstrings of the invading Assyrian army.</note>, by whom Sennacherib <note>The powerful King of Assyria (reigned 705–681 BC) famous for his siege of Jerusalem.</note> was put to flight, [counted] 341 genera-

<summary>This opening page introduces the study of ancient history, noting how early civilizations often exaggerated their own age and lineage to gain prestige. It specifically references Herodotus’s account of Egyptian chronology and the long succession of kings from Menes to the defeat of Sennacherib.</summary>

<keywords>Herodotus, Egypt, Menes, Sethon, Sennacherib, chronology, antiquity, historical origins, Assyria</keywords>

<page-num>2</page-num>
<header>CONCERNING ANTIQUITIES</header>
<meta>catchword: generations</meta>

generations or successions of men, as well as an equal number of Priests of Vulcan <note>The Roman name for the Greek Hephaestus; in an Egyptian context, Herodotus refers to the priests of the god Ptah at Memphis.</note>, and Kings of Egypt. For three hundred of these successions he sets 10,000 years; for, *according to his saying*, the lifespan of three generations makes up 100 years: and adding to these 10,000 years another 1,340 for the remaining 41 generations, the entire time from Menes to Sethon would amount to 11,340 years. By following this method of calculation, and attributing a longer reign to the Gods of Egypt than to the Kings who came after them, that writer further tells us—from the mouths of those same Priests—that 15,000 years passed between Pan <note>Likely the Egyptian god Min.</note> and Amosis, and 17,000 years between the latter and Hercules <note>Likely the Egyptian god Khonsu or Shu.</note>. The Chaldeans <note>An ancient people of Mesopotamia, famous in antiquity for their developments in astronomy and astrology.</note> did not yield to the Egyptians in this boasting: for *Callisthenes*, the disciple of *Aristotle*, sent astronomical observations from Babylon to Greece, which were said to have begun 1,903 years before the time of Alexander the Great. But the Chaldeans themselves boasted much more, saying that they had observed the course of the stars for 473,000 years. Thus there were also those who placed the Kingdoms of Assyria, Media, and Damascus much earlier than the truth allowed.

Some Greeks called the times before the reign of Ogyges <note>A mythical primeval king of Attica or Boeotia; the "Flood of Ogyges" was considered the first great deluge in Greek myth.</note> "unknown," because they had no historical writings from that era; those between his flood and the institution of the Olympic Games they called "fabulous" <note>Meaning "mythological" or "legendary."</note>, because the history of that time was mixed with many poetic fables; and those after the beginning of the Olympiads <note>The four-year periods between the Olympic Games, used by the Greeks as a calendar system starting traditionally in 776 BC.</note> they called "historical," because the historical accounts were then purged of such fables. The fabulous ages lack a reliable <term>chronology</term> <note>The science of dating historical events.</note>, as do the historical ones during the first 60 or 70 Olympiads.

Before the flourishing of the Persian monarchy, Europe had no formal chronology; and all those we now have from earlier centuries have been fashioned since that time from conjectures and reasoning. At the beginning of that monarchy, *Acusilaus* <note>An early Greek historian and logographer from Argos, active around 500 BC.</note> placed Phoroneus <note>Regarded in Greek myth as the first man or first king of Argos.</note> as old as Ogyges and his flood, and placed that flood 1,020 years before the first Olympiad, which is more than 680 years older than the truth; and to make this calculation valid—

<summary>This page critiques the exaggerated chronologies of the ancient Egyptians and Chaldeans, who claimed tens of thousands of years of history. It also categorizes Greek history into unknown, fabulous, and historical periods, noting the lack of reliable dating before the Persian era.</summary>

<keywords>Egypt, Chaldeans, Callisthenes, Aristotle, Ogyges, Olympiads, Persian Monarchy, Acusilaus, Phoroneus, ancient chronology, historical criticism</keywords>

[to] make, later writers have multiplied both the number and the years of the Kings. *Plutarch (b)* tells us that the philosophers of old shared their views in verse, like Orpheus, Hesiod, Parmenides, Xenophanes, Empedocles, and Thales; but that they later abandoned the use of poetry: and that Aristarchus, Timocharis, Aristillus, and Hipparchus did not diminish astronomy by writing about it in prose, after Eudoxus, Hesiod, and Thales had sung of it in verse. ### OF THE GREEKS.
<sig>A 2</sig>

later writers have multiplied both the number and the years of the Kings. *Plutarch* (b) tells us that the philosophers of old shared their sentiments in verse, such as Orpheus, Hesiod, Parmenides, Xenophanes, Empedocles, and Thales; but that they later abandoned the use of poetry. He further notes that Aristarchus, Timocharis, Aristillus, and Hipparchus did not diminish the prestige of astronomy by writing about it in prose, after Eudoxus, Hesiod, and Thales had sung of it in verse. Solon also wrote in meter (c), and the Seven Sages of Greece <note>A group of 7th–6th century BCE philosophers, statesmen, and lawgivers renowned for their wisdom</note> were, according to the testimony of *Anaximenes* (d), all inclined toward poetry. Until this time, then, the Greeks wrote only in verse, and therefore there could be no chronology or any history except that which was adorned with poetic flourishes. *Pliny* (e), naming the first inventors of all things, relates that under the reign of Cyrus, Pherecydes of Syros taught how to set down discourses, and Cadmus of *Miletus* how to set down histories in *prose*. And in another place (f) he says that *Cadmus of Miletus was the first who wrote in prose*. *Josephus* (g) now testifies that *Cadmus of Miletus* and *Acusilaus* lived only a short time before the expedition of the Persians against the Greeks: while *Suidas* says (h) that *Acusilaus* was a most ancient historian, and that he copied genealogies from copper tables which, as it was told, had been found by his father in a corner of his house. Who hid them there may rightly be doubted; for the Greeks had no public records or inscriptions older than Draco's laws (i) <note>Draco was an Athenian lawmaker (c. 621 BCE) known for his extremely harsh legal code</note>. Under the reign of Darius Hystaspes, or shortly thereafter, Pherecydes of *Athens* wrote about the antiquities and ancient lineages of the Athenians in ten books. He was one of the first and best of this sort of writer among the Europeans, for which reason he earned the name <term>The Genealogist</term> <note>A scholar specializing in the study of family lineages and ancient origins</note>; and *Dionysius of Halicarnassus* says (k) that he was equaled by none of the other genealogists. *Epimenides*, not the philosopher but a historian, also wrote

# OF THE ANTIQUITIES

...of the ancient families: and **Hellanicus**, who was twelve years older than **Herodotus**, arranged the chronology of his history according to the successions of the Priestesses of Argive Juno <note>The high priestesses of the Temple of Hera at Argos served as a standard reference for dating events in early Greek history</note>. Others calculated the times according to the reigns of the Princes (*l*) of Athens, or the Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> Kings. **Hippias of Elis** published a short list of the Olympiads; but without supporting those with any certain proofs, as **Plutarch** testifies (*m*); he lived in the hundred and fifth Olympiad, and was mocked by **Plato** for his ignorance. It seems this list contained nothing other than a short account of the victors in each Olympiad. After him, **Ephorus** (*n*), the pupil of **Isocrates**, compiled a chronological history of Greece, which, beginning with the return of the **Heraclids** <note>The legendary descendants of Hercules who were said to have conquered the Peloponnesus</note> into Peloponnesus and ending with the siege of Perinthus in the twentieth year of Philip, the father of Alexander the Great—that is, eleven years before the fall of the Persian monarchy. In this work, he calculated the time by generations (*o*); for the calculation according to the Olympiads, or any other fixed point in time (*p*), was not yet in use among the Greeks. The **Arundel marbles** <note>Also known as the Parian Chronicle, these are inscribed marble slabs recording a Greek chronology from 1582 BCE to 264 BCE</note> were erected sixty years after the death of Alexander, in the fourth year of the hundred and twenty-eighth Olympiad; in these, mention is made neither of the Olympiads, nor of any other established point in time, but the events are placed in their order by counting backwards from that time. About this time, however, they began to set down the times in years, and in the following Olympiad that calculation was further continued by **Timaeus of Sicily**: for he wrote a history, in several books, up to his own age; in which he compared the years and successions of the Rulers (*q*) and Kings of Sparta, the Princes of Athens, and the Priestesses of Argos, with those of the victors in the Olympic games, in order to reconcile the Olympiads, the years and successions of the Kings and Priestesses, and the poetic histories, according to his best judgment, with each other—

### OF THE GREEKS.

Since this chronology has been constructed by bringing together the times of the Spartan Kings—or rather, their number—it pleases us to examine that calculation.

The Egyptians, Greeks, and Latins calculated the reigns of their Princes as being of equal duration to human generations, and they counted three generations to a hundred years, as we stated above <gloss>original: (z)</gloss>; so that they give each Prince an average of thirty-three years of rule, or even more. For the seven Kings of Rome, who preceded the Mayors <gloss>original: (a) Consuls</gloss> <note>The text uses the Dutch term *Burgemeeſters* (Mayors) to describe the Roman Consuls who led the Republic after the kings were expelled</note>, they set down 244 years, which is 35 years for each; for the first twelve Kings of Sicyon <note>An ancient city-state in the Peloponnese</note>, such as **Aegialeus**, **Europs**, etc., they allow 529 years, which is 44 years for each; for the first eight Kings of **Argos**, **Inachus**, **Phoroneus**, etc., they allow 371 years, which is more than 46 years for each. From the return of the **Heraclidae** <note>The "Return of the Heraclidae" is a legendary event in which the descendants of Hercules reclaimed their ancestral lands in the Peloponnese</note> into the Peloponnese until the end of the first Messenian War, ten Kings of one line ruled at Sparta, namely **Eurysthenes**, **Agis**, **Echestratus**, **Labotas**, **Doryssus**, **Agesilaus**, **Archelaus**, **Teleclus**, **Alcamenes**, and **Polydorus**; and nine from another royal house \*, namely **Procles**, **Soos**, **Eurypon**, **Prytanis**, **Eunomus**, **Polydectes**, **Charilaus**, **Nicander**, and **Theopompus**. During that same time, there were these ten Kings at Messene: **Cresphontes**, **Aepytus**, **Glaucus**, **Isthmius**, **Dotadas**, **Sibotas**, **Phintas**, **Antiochus**, **Euphaes**, and **Aristodemus**; and in Arcadia these nine: **Cypselus**, **Oleas**, **Buchalion**, **Phialus**, **Simus**, **Pompus**, **Aegineta**, **Polymnestor**, and **Echmis**. The duration of the reigns of all these Princes amounts, according to the chronologists, to 379 years; that is roughly 38 years for each of the ten, and 42 years for each of the nine Kings. The five Kings of Lacedaemon <note>Another name for Sparta</note> from the line of **Eurysthenes**, who ruled between the end of the first Messenian War and the beginning of the reign of **Darius Hystaspes** <note>The Persian Great King, r. 522–486 BCE</note>, and who were named **Eurycrates**, **Anaxander**, **Eurycrates II**, **Leon**, and **Anaxandrides**, are said to have possessed the throne for 202 years, which is more than 40 years on average.

### ON ANTIQUITIES

The **Greek chronologists** <note>Time-reckoners or historians who specialized in dating events.</note>, who followed **Timaeus** and **Eratosthenes** on this footing, have given the Kings of various cities who lived before the times of the **Persian monarchy** <note>The Achaemenid Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great.</note> an average of 35 to 40 years of rule each—a duration that so far exceeds the natural course of things that one cannot grant it any belief. If we observe the findings in history, we see that Princes, one with another, rule for approximately 18 or 20 years: though it may happen that in one country one finds five or six years more for each, in another country they rule for just as much shorter a time. Eighteen or twenty years can be set as a midpoint.

The eighteen Kings of **Judah**, who followed **Solomon**, ruled for 390 years, which is twenty-one and two-thirds years on average. The fifteen Kings of **Israel**, after Solomon’s death, ruled for 259 years, which is seventeen and one-fourth years on average. The eighteen Kings of **Babylon**, such as **Nabonassar** etc., ruled for 209 years, which is eleven and two-thirds years on average. The ten Kings of **Persia**, **Cyrus**, **Cambyses** etc., ruled for 208 years, which is twenty and four-fifths years on average. The sixteen successors of **Alexander the Great**, and of his brother and son, who ruled in **Syria** after the **Greek monarchy** was divided into various kingdoms—such as **Seleucus**, **Antiochus Soter** etc.—ruled for 244 years, which is fifteen and one-fourth years on average. The eleven Kings of **Egypt**, calculated from the same point in time, such as **Ptolemy Lagus** <note>The founder of the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt and a general of Alexander the Great.</note> etc., ruled for 277 years, which is over 25 years on average. The eight Kings of **Macedonia**, **Cassander** etc., ruled for 138 years, which is seventeen and one-fourth years on average. The thirty Kings of **England**, such as **William the Conqueror**, **William Rufus** <note>original: "Willem de Rosse" (William the Red). He was the son of William the Conqueror.</note>, etc., ruled for 648 years, which is twenty-one and a half years on average. The first twenty-four Kings of **France**, **Pharamond** <note>A legendary early king of the Franks.</note> etc., ruled for 458 years, which is 19 years on average; the second twenty-four, **Louis the Stammerer** etc., 451 years, which is eighteen and three-fourths years on average; and the following fifteen, **Philip of Valois**, etc., 315 years, which is 21 years on average; and these sixty-three kings...

...who waged the Messenian war <note>The First Messenian War (c. 743–724 BC in traditional dating) was a conflict between Sparta and Messenia.</note> (*b*), was descended in the fifth generation from Oiolikus, the son of Theras and brother-in-law of Aristodemus, who, according to *Pausanias* (*c*), was the <term>guardian: "momboir" in the original, referring to a legal protector or tutor for minors.</term> over the children of the latter; so that from the return of the Heraclids <note>The "Return of the Heraclids" is a traditional event in Greek mythology where the descendants of the hero Hercules returned to the Peloponnese to reclaim their ancestral kingdoms.</note>, which occurred during the life of Theras, until the battle fought in the fifth year of this war, there are six generations, and for each of these—which, in my opinion, were mostly through the eldest sons—one cannot well set more than 30 years, which together makes 170 or 180 years. That war then lasted 19 or 20 years; if one adds the last 15 years to the average calculation of the aforementioned number, the end of that war will be about 190 years after the return of the Heraclids: whereas the followers of *Timaeus* <note>Timaeus of Tauromenium was a Greek historian who first used the Olympiads as a system for dating historical events.</note> place 390 years between those two points in time, and thus more than 60 years for every generation.

From these proofs it appears that the chronologists have made the time between the return of the Heraclids and the end of the first Messenian war about 190 years longer than it actually was: and thus they have also erred regarding the time that passed from that war until the rise of the Persian monarchy, as will appear from the following account. Leonidas was defeated by the Persians at Thermopylae in the sixth year of Xerxes; and Leutychides II fled shortly thereafter from Sparta to Tegea, where he died. Now, calculate these three hundred years back from the end of the aforementioned war, and the legislation of Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver who established the military-oriented reformation of Spartan society.</note> will fall within the nineteenth Olympiad: and if one calculates according to Socrates' saying, possibly with the twenty-second or twenty-third. *Athenaeus* <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian writing around 200 AD.</note> tells us from older writers ([*i*]), such as *Hellanicus*, *Sosimus*, and *Hieronymus*, that Lycurgus the lawgiver was a contemporary of Terpander the Musician; and that Terpander was the first who achieved victory in a solemn musical contest which was established in the twenty-sixth Olympiad during the festival days of the Carnea <note>A major religious festival in Sparta dedicated to Apollo Carneus.</note>. This Terpander triumphed four times in those Pythian games <note>Games held at Delphi in honor of Apollo; they were the second most important after the Olympics.</note>, so that he lived at least until the twenty-ninth Olympiad: and while he began to flourish in Lycurgus's days, it is not probable that this lawgiver was in his prime before the eighteenth Olympiad. 

Because the name of Lycurgus was found on the Olympic discus, *Aristotle* concluded that he accompanied Iphitus in the restoration of the Olympic games, and this opinion of *Aristotle* may be the ground upon which the chronologers have made Lycurgus and Iphitus <note>The King of Elis who is said to have revived the Olympic Games in 776 BC.</note> contemporaries. But Iphitus did not restore all the Olympic games at once. It is true he restored the first footrace in the first Olympiad ([*k*]) when Coroebus carried away the prize: but in the fourteenth Olympiad, the double footrace was added to the games, in which Hypenus triumphed; and in the eighteenth, the <term>Quinquertium</term> <note>The Latin term for the Pentathlon, a contest of five events: running, jumping, discus throw, javelin throw, and wrestling.</note> and the wrestling, in which Lampus and Eurybates, two Spartans, achieved the victory: and the throwing of the Discus or plate was one of the games belonging to the <term>Quinquertium</term>. *Pausanias* <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD, famous for his "Description of Greece."</note> tells us ([*l*]), that there were three throwing-disks preserved in the Olympic treasury at Altis <note>The sacred grove at Olympia.</note>; and these, having the name of Lycurgus upon them, showed that they were by him, at the institution of the

The *Quinquertium* <note>original: "Quinquertium"; the Latin term for the Pentathlon, an athletic contest consisting of five events.</note> had been established in the eighteenth Olympiad: but let us press this chronology even further.

Polydectes, the King of Sparta, being slain before the birth of his son Charillus (or Charilaus), left his kingdom to his brother Lycurgus, who after the birth of Charillus became his guardian <term>momboir: a legal guardian or regent for a minor</term>. When Charillus was about eight months old, Lycurgus undertook a journey to Crete and Asia while his orphan ward grew up. Upon his return, he brought back the poems of Homer and shortly thereafter—supposedly in the twenty-second or twenty-third Olympiad (for he had by then grown old)—he promulgated his laws. Terpander the Lyric Poet began to flourish around this time; for he followed Orpheus and Homer ([*m*]), sang the poems of the latter alongside his own, set the laws of Lycurgus to verse, and was the victor in the Pythian games of the twenty-sixth Olympiad, as we mentioned above. He was the first who distinguished the modes of lyrical songs by their names. Andalus <note>Likely a reference to Olympus the Mysian, a legendary flute player often paired with Clonas.</note> and Clonas did the same shortly thereafter in wind music <note>Music played on pipes or flutes, such as the aulos.</note>. From this time forward, as the arts of poetry and music were nurtured through the Pythian games, one saw various illustrious Poets and Musicians appear in Greece: such as Archilochus, Eumelus, Corinthius, Polymnestus, Thaletas, Xenodemus, Xenocritus, Sacadas, Tyrtaeus, Telesilla, Rhianus, Alcman, Arion, Stesichorus, Mimnermus, Alcaeus, Sappho, Theognis, Anacreon, Ibycus, Simonides, Aeschylus, and Pindar, by whom the poetry and music of the Greeks were brought to perfection.

Lycurgus promulgated his laws under the reign of Agesilaus, the son and successor of Doryssus, in the line of Spartan Kings who descended from Eurysthenes. Pausanias *(q)* relates that Melas, the son of Antissus (from the lineage of Gonussa, the daughter of Sicyon), lived no more than six generations before Cypselus the King of Corinth, and that he was a contemporary of Aletes, who returned to the Peloponnese with the Heraclidae. In the first attempt the Heraclidae made to return, Eurystheus—who lived at the same time as Hercules—was slain by Hyllus. Hyllus himself was struck down in their second attempt, Cleodius in their third, and Aristomachus in their fourth; and Aristodemus died shortly after their return, leaving the Kingdom of Lacedemon <note>Lacedemon is the ancient name for the city-state of Sparta and its surrounding territory.</note> to his sons Eurysthenes and Procles. Elissa is indeed Dido, and Carthage was destroyed when Lentulus and Mummius were Consuls <margin>consuls</margin>, that is, in the year 4568 of the Julian period <term>Julian Period: a chronological system starting in 4713 BCE, used by scholars to synchronize different calendars</term>. If one counts back 737 years from that year, then the *Enkaenia* <note>original: "Enkaenia"; a Greek term for a dedication or consecration ceremony</note> or founding of Carthage occurred in the fifteenth year of Pygmalion, the King of Tyre and brother of Dido. She fled in the seventh year of that Prince; but the Carthaginian chronology only began from the day of the city's dedication. *Virgil* and his commentator <margin>scholiast</margin> *Servius*, who possibly obtained a portion of their information from Tyrian and Cypriot records as well as those of Carthage, relate that Teucer, in the days of Dido—shortly before the reign of her brother Pygmalion—arrived in Cyprus from the Trojan War; and with the help of Dido's father, he seized that island and drove out Cinyras. The Arundel Marbles <note>The Parian Chronicle, an ancient Greek timeline inscribed on marble, once part of the collection of the Earl of Arundel</note> say that Teucer landed in Cyprus seven years after the destruction of Troy and built the city of Salamis: and *Apollodorus* testifies that Cinyras married Metharme, the daughter of Pygmalion, and founded Paphos. It is therefore credible that the Romans in the time of Augustus did not entirely follow the technical chronology of *Eratosthenes* <note>a Greek scholar who calculated one of the most famous ancient timelines</note>; but drew these matters from the records of Carthage, Tyre, and Cyprus; and according to those, Teucer landed in Cyprus during the reign of Pygmalion's ancestor, or about 76 years after Solomon's death.

*Dionysius of Halicarnassus* says <margin>Book 1, page 15</margin> that Latinus, during the Trojan War, ruled over the Aborigines <note>the 'Aborigines' here refers to the earliest mythical inhabitants of central Italy, rather than indigenous Australians</note> in Italy, and that Rome was built by Romulus in the sixteenth age after that war. By these "ages" he means the successive reigns of Princes; for immediately after Latinus, he counts sixteen Kings, the last of whom is Numitor, in whose days Rome was founded.

After Romulus until the reign of the Consuls <margin>(v) *Consuls.*</margin> (v), *Dionysius* <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian who wrote about Roman history</note> along with others places six Kings of Rome, and thus 22 Kings starting from Latinus <note>The legendary king of the Latins for whom the language and people were named</note>; for Romulus and Numitor were contemporaries. If one calculates these 22 reigns at an average of 18 years each—as many of these princes were slain—they amount to 396 years; and these years, counted backward from Junius Brutus and Valerius Publicola, the first two Consuls, show that the Trojan War was waged about 78 years after Solomon.

The expedition of Sesostris <note>A legendary King of Egypt, often associated by early historians with Ramses II or Senusret III</note> against Greece occurred one generation earlier than that of the Argonauts: for when that Prince returned to Egypt, he left Aeëtes in Colchis, who ruled there until the expedition of the Argonauts; and Prometheus, whom he placed with a body of troops at Mount Caucasus to guard that pass, was freed from that duty and set at liberty thirty years later by Hercules. Phlias and Eumedon, the sons of the great Bacchus (as the Poets named Sesostris) and of Ariadne the daughter of Minos, were also among the Argonauts. When Sesostris was on his return journey to Egypt, his brother Danaus fled from him to Greece in a long ship with his 50 daughters. The ship *Argos* was built after the design of this ship, and Argus the son of Danaus was its master builder. Neptune, the brother and Admiral of Sesostris, fathered with Amymone, one of Danaus's daughters, Nauplius the Argonaut, whom she bore in Greece: and two other daughters of Danaus married Archander and Archilites, the sons of Achæus, who himself was born of Creusa, the daughter of the Athenian King Erechtheus; so that the daughters of Danaus were three generations younger than Erechtheus, and consequently contemporary with Theseus the son of Aegeus, the latter having been adopted as a son by Pandion the son of Erechtheus. Egypt was first, like other lands, divided into several small lordships, and was by degrees unified into one Kingdom. The father of Solomon’s wife <note>This refers to the unnamed Pharaoh in 1 Kings who captured Gezer</note> was the first King of Egypt who entered Phoenicia with an army; in which expedition he only captured Gezer and gave it to his daughter. The Holy Scriptures do not mention any preceding King of Egypt who, ruling over all these nations, marched out of his land to make conquests; indeed, the Holy history, from Abraham until Solomon, excludes such a conqueror. The Shepherd Kings <note>The Hyksos, a group of foreign rulers who governed Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period</note> ruled for a long time in Lower Egypt and were, according to *Manetho* <note>An Egyptian priest and historian from the 3rd century BCE</note>, only driven out just before the building of Solomon's Temple; so that, while they inhabited Lower Egypt, the upper part was ruled by other Kings. As long as Egypt was divided into various lordships, there could be no other King of all Egypt like Sesostris; and no historian places his life after the time of Shishak: so that the names Sesostris and Shishak undoubtedly belonged to one person. This opinion is not new; for *Josephus* maintains it where he says:

> "that *Herodotus* erred in attributing Shishak's deeds to Sesostris, and that his error was only in the name of the King;" For this is the same as if he said, "The correct name of the Egyptian King whose deeds *Herodotus* describes is Shishak; and he errs only in calling him Sesostris, or he calls him Sesostris by a corruption of his true name."

Before the exact length of the solar year was known, all nations reckoned their months by the course of the moon, and their years according to the successions of summer and winter, autumn and spring <margin>*(e) Genesis 1:14 & 8:22. Censorinus, [The Birthday Book] ch. 18 & 19. Cicero, Against Verres. Geminus, ch. 6.*</margin> *(e)*. In making almanacs or calendars for their festivals, they used the nearest whole numbers, setting thirty days to a month and twelve months to a year; this is the origin of the division of the celestial circle into 360 degrees. When Noah could not see the moon during the flood, he therefore reckoned thirty days for a month; but if the new moon appeared one or two days before the end of the month, they began the new month on the first day of its appearance <margin>*(f) Cicero, Against Verres.*</margin> *(f)*. And this was a general practice until the Egyptians of Thebes discovered the length of the solar year. For this reason, Diodorus <margin>*(g) [Library of History] 1.50.*</margin> *(g)* says: "the Egyptians of Thebes do not use intercalary <note>Intercalary months or days are extra periods inserted into a calendar to make it align with the solar year (the time it takes Earth to orbit the sun)</note> months, nor do they subtract any days [from the months], as is the custom among most Greeks." *Cicero* also says <margin>*(h) Against Verres.*</margin> *(h)*: <note>original Latin: "Est consuetudo Siculorum caeterorumque Graecorum, quod suos dies mensesque congraere volunt cum Solis Lunaeque ratione, ut nonnumquam siquid discrepet, eximant unum aliquem diem aut summum biduum ex mesne [civili dierum triginta] quos illi. ἐξαιρεσίμους dies nominant."</note> "It is the custom of the Sicilians and other Greeks, because they wish their days and months to agree with the logic of the Sun and Moon, that if any discrepancy arises, they sometimes remove one day or at most two from the [civil month of thirty] days, which they call <term>ἐξαιρεσίμους</term> <note>original: "exairesimous," a Greek term for "exempted" or "omitted" days used to keep lunar months in sync with the solar year</note> days." For the intention of the ancients was to conduct the months according to the moon, and the years according to the sun. For that which was commanded by the laws and the oracles—to sacrifice according to 'the three' <note>This refers to the *Trieteris*, a cycle meant to harmonize lunar and solar time for religious purposes.</note>, namely the ancestral traditions of months, days, and years—was understood by all the Greeks as keeping the years in harmony with the sun, and the days and months with the moon. Keeping the years by the sun means that the same sacrifices to the gods are performed at the same seasons of the year, so that the spring sacrifice is always held during the spring, the summer sacrifice during the summer, and likewise that the same sacrifices fall in the other seasons of the year. For they believed this to be pleasing and agreeable to the gods. This could not happen unless the solstices and equinoxes occurred at the same points in the calendar. And keeping the days according to the moon is this: that the naming of the days follows the phases of the moon's light. For the names of the days were derived from the moon’s illumination. On the day the new moon appears, it was called 'new-month-day' <note>original: *neomenia* / νεομηνία</note> by contraction; the day it makes its second appearance they called 'the second'; and the phase of the moon occurring in the middle of the month they called 'the month-divider' <note>original: *dichomenia* / διχομηνία, typically the full moon</note> from the occurrence itself. And generally, they named all the days from the moon’s illuminations. Thus also the thirtieth day of the month, being the last, they called 'the thirtieth' <note>original: *triakas* / τριακάδα</note> from the occurrence itself.

### OF ANTIQUITIES
<meta>catchword: moon-</meta>

...[ordering] <note>The Dutch suffix "-nende" suggests a preceding mention of Solon "ordering" or "arranging" these matters.</note>, calls that day *the old and the new* <note>original: *ἕνη καὶ νέα*</note>, that is, the last day of the old and the first of the new month: for he introduced months of twenty-nine and thirty days alternately, making the first day of the new month begin on the last of the old.

To the twelve lunar months the ancient Greeks added a thirteenth <margin>(*n*)</margin> every other year, and this insertion made their *Dieteris* <term>Dieteris: A two-year cycle used to align lunar months with the solar year</term>; but because that reckoning made the year nearly one month too long over eight years, no month was inserted in the eighth year, by which their *Oktaeteris* <term>Oktaeteris: An eight-year cycle</term> (of which the *Tetraeteris* <term>Tetraeteris: A four-year cycle</term> was the half) came to be: and it appears that these periods were almost as old as the Greek religions, since they were used in several of their *Sacra* <note>original: *Sakra*; sacred rites or mysteries</note> or God-consecrated secrets. The *Oktaeteris* was the great year of Cadmus and Minos <margin>(*o*)</margin>, and was apparently brought into Greece and Crete by the Phoenicians, who came from the south with Cadmus and Europa, where it remained in use until the days of Herodotus: for this writer, calculating the length of time of seventy years <margin>(*p*)</margin>, counts thirty days in a lunar month, and twelve such months, or three hundred and sixty days, in the ordinary year, without adding the intercalated months each time; which he finally adds to the total time as a number of twenty-five. And corresponding with the number of days in the calendar year of the Greeks, the Athenians erected three hundred and sixty statues for Demetrius Phalereus. But so that the months would better coincide with the course of the moon, the old custom of inserting one month every other year was changed by the Greeks Cleostratus, Harpalus, and others, during the time of the Persian monarchy; and they inserted three months in every *Oktaeteris*; until Meton invented the nineteen-year cycle, in which seven months were joined.

### OF THE GREEKS.
D
<meta>catchword: The-</meta>

...[y year] <note>The previous page ends with "ordinar-", implying "ordinary year".</note> consisted of months, and that, to reconcile the length of the solar year, a thirteenth month was inserted now and then. The ancient year of the Egyptians was no different, until the time of Hyperion or Osiris <note>Osiris is a major Egyptian god associated with the afterlife and fertility; Hyperion is a Greek Titan, often identified with the sun</note>, King of Egypt and father of Helios and Selene, or Horus and Bubastis: for the Jews brought this calendar reckoning from Egypt with them; and *Diodorus* says (*s*) that Uranus, the father of Hyperion, used this year; and that the priests of Osiris's temple filled three hundred and sixty bowls with milk in that temple every day (*t*): I think he means one bowl each day, and thus three hundred and sixty in total; so as to reckon the days of their calendar year, and to find the difference between that and the true solar year.

That the Jews used the luni-solar year <term>luni-solar year: A calendar based on the phases of the moon but adjusted to stay in sync with the solar seasons</term> is beyond dispute. Their months began with the new moon: and they called their first month *Abib*, because of the corn harvest <note>In historical texts, "corn" refers to grain in general, such as barley or wheat</note>, which then commenced. The Passover festival was held on the fourteenth day of that first month, when the moon was full: and if the corn was not then ripe enough for the offering of the firstfruits, the festival day was postponed, and a month was inserted between the last of the old and the first of the new year. The harvest was always gathered before Pentecost, and the other fruits before the Feast of Tabernacles.

*Simplicius* <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator</note>, in his commentary on the *Physical Auscultation* <note>original: *Physicales Acroasis*; referring to Aristotle's *Physics*</note> of *Aristotle*, says (*u*) "Some begin the year at the summer solstice, like the people of Attica; some at the autumnal equinox <note>original: *middelbaren nacht des herfsts*, literally "middle-night of autumn"</note>, like the Asians; some in the winter, like the Romans; and others around the spring equinox, like the Arabs and the inhabitants of Damascus: and with some the month begins with the new moon, with others with the full moon." From this it appears that all nations reckoned by luni-solar years, and determined their beginning, as much as they were able, according to the four seasons. <page-num>26</page-num>
->CONCERNING ANTIQUITIES<-

In this regard <note>The OCR reads "December," but context and the previous page's catchword suggest a word like "Dezerhalve" (Therefore) or "Dezelve" (In the same way).</note> it seems to me that the Romans formerly began their year in the spring, although it was later pushed back to the winter. The ancient civil year of the Assyrians and Babylonians was, like that of other nations, also regulated according to the course of the moon: for the Samaritans, who came from various parts of the Assyrian monarchy, used that year; and the Jews, who returned from their captivity in Babylon, named the months of their lunisolar year with the names of the Babylonian year. *Berosus* says (*w*) also that the Babylonians celebrated their festival *Sakraea* <note>The Sacaea; a festival similar to the Roman Saturnalia where slaves and masters swapped roles</note> on the sixteenth of the month Lous (a lunar month of the Macedonians), and fixed it to one season: and the Arabs, a nation by which Babylon was populated, still use lunar months to this day. *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> testifies (*x*), that the *Sarus* <term>Sarus: An ancient Babylonian unit of time</term> of the Chaldeans contained 222 months, that is eighteen years of twelve lunar months, plus six months that were intercalated <note>Intercalation is the practice of adding extra time to a calendar to keep it synchronized with the seasons</note> between them. And it seems that Cyrus (*y*), when he diverted the river Gindus <note>The Gyndes, modern-day Diyala River</note> into 360 channels, alluded to the number of days of which the calendar year of the Medes and Persians consisted. Therefore, the Emperor *Julian* said (*z*), “While all nations, to put it in a word, align their months with the course of the moon, we alone, with the Egyptians, make the days of the year equal to the course of the sun.”

The Egyptians, applying themselves more and more to trade and navigation, began for the sake of these to practice astronomy, and by observing the daily rising and setting of the stars, they finally found that the true solar year was five days longer than their common calendar year; so that they added five days to their 12 months of 30 days. *Strabo* (*a*) and *Diodorus* (*b*) say that the Egyptians of Thebes <note>An ancient capital of Egypt</note> discovered this course of the sun: these are the words of the former: “It is said that the Priests of Thebes are experienced above others in astronomy and philosophy. They invented the art of calculating the year not according to the course...”

# OF THE GREEKS.

D 2

> “ ...the course of the moon, but to regulate it according to that of the sun: and to 
> “ twelve months, each of 30 days, they annually added
> “ five days. ”

In memory of this improvement of the year, those five added days were dedicated to Osiris, Isis, Horus the elder, Typhon, and Nephthys the wife of Typhon <gloss>(c)</gloss>: the Egyptians feigning <note>In this context, "feigning" means creating a myth or poetic allegory</note> that the year was increased by those days upon the birth of those persons; that is, under the reign of Ouranus or Ammon, the father of Sesak <note>The author likely refers to Shishak, the Egyptian Pharaoh mentioned in the Bible</note>. In the burial place of Amenophis <gloss>(d)</gloss>, who reigned shortly thereafter, they also made a golden circle of 365 cubits in its circumference, and divided into 365 equal parts, to represent the days of the year; and upon each part the rising and setting of the stars occurring on that day was noted; and this circle remained in existence until the time that Cambyses <note>Cambyses II, the Persian king who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE</note> made himself master of Egypt. Until the reign of Ouranus, the father of Hyperion, and grandfather of Helius and Selene (that is, of Ammon, the father of Osiris or Sesak, and grandfather of Horus and Bubaste), the Egyptians used the ancient lunisolar year: but under his reign the Egyptians of Thebes began to apply themselves to navigation and astronomy, found the true length of the solar year by observing the daily rising and setting of the stars, added five days to their old calendar year, and dedicated them to his five children named above. And when they, through further observations, had sufficiently discovered the time of the solstices, they were able to place the beginning of their New Year at the midnight of the spring <note>Referring to the vernal equinox</note>. This reckoning of the year, finally brought into Chaldea, gave birth to that of Nabonassar <note>Nabonassar was a King of Babylon; his reign marks the beginning of the "Era of Nabonassar," a chronological era used by ancient astronomers like Ptolemy</note>: because the years of Nabonassar and those of Egypt began on one day, called by them Thoth, and they were in all respects identical. The first year of Nabonassar began on the 26th of February of the old Roman year, 740 years before the common era of Christ, and 33 days and 5 hours before the midnight of the spring according to the mean motion of the sun:

because it is not probable that the distinction between its true and apparent motion was already known in the infancy of astronomy. When one calculates that a year of 365 days is 5 hours and 49 minutes shorter than the time in which the sun completes its course; thus the beginning of this year, in 137 years, must have receded 33 days and 5 hours; and consequently, it began in Egypt first at the midnight of the spring <note>the vernal equinox</note> (being determined according to the apparent motion of the sun) 137 years before the Era of Nabonassar; that is, in the 3830th year of the Julian Period, or 96 years after the death of Solomon: and if one placed its first day on that following the midnight of the spring, it could have begun four years earlier: and around this time the reign of Amenophis ended: for he did not come from Susa to the Trojan War, but died afterwards in Egypt. This chronological system was adopted by the Persians from the Babylonians; the Greeks also used it in the Era of Philip <gloss>(e)</gloss>, which began with the death of Alexander the Great: and Julius Caesar improved it, by inserting one day every fourth year, and had it adopted by the Romans.

Syncellus <note>George Syncellus, a 9th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> says that the five mentioned days were added to the old year of the Egyptians by the last King of the shepherds <note>The "shepherd kings" or Hyksos, who ruled Egypt before the New Kingdom</note>: and the difference between his and our opinion is very small; for the reign of the shepherds ended only one or two generations before Amenophis lengthened the year. One should note, however, that the shepherds did not love arts or sciences.

The beginning of the first month of the lunisolar years, due to the intercalated month, often fell fourteen days before or fourteen days after the equinoxes and solstices. This was the reason that the astronomers, who first formed the celestial sphere, placed the points of the equinoxes \* and solstices in the middle of the signs of Aries, Cancer, Chelae <term>Chelae (the Claws of Scorpio, anciently used to represent the constellation Libra)</term> and Capricorn. When the celestial sphere was first formed, the summer solstice was in the fifteenth degree, or the middle of the constellation of Cancer; after that, it moved to the twelfth, and subsequently to the eighth, fourth, and first degree. *Eudoxus*, who flourished about sixty years after *Meton*, and a hundred years before *Aratus*, describing the *sphere* of the ancients, placed the points of the solstices and equinoxes † in the middle of the constellations of Aries, Cancer, Chelae <note>original: "Chelae", the Claws of the Scorpion, which the ancients used for the constellation we now call Libra</note>, and Capricorn, as is testified by *Hipparchus of Bithynia* (*e*); and also appears from the description of the equator and the two tropics, which was copied by *Aratus* from *Eudoxus* (*f*); as well as from the placement of the circles (*g*) <note>the colures</note> of the equinoxes and solstices which, in the sphere of *Eudoxus* described by *Hipparchus*, turn through the middle of the aforementioned constellations: For *Hipparchus* says that *Eudoxus* drew the circle of the solstices through the middle of the Great Bear, the middle of Cancer, the neck of Hydrus, the star between the stern and the mast of Argo, the tail of the Southern Fish, the middle of Capricorn, and Sagitta, the neck and the left wing of the Swan, and the left hand of Cepheus: and that he drew the circle of the equinoxes through the left hand of Arctophylax <note>original: "Arktofylax", also known as Boötes, the Herdsman</note>, along the middle of his body, straight through the middle of Chelae, through the right hand and fore-knee of the Centaur, the bend of Eridanus, the head of Cetus, straight through the back of Aries, and through the head and right hand of Perseus.

The Sidonians were always in possession of the trade on the Mediterranean Sea, as far as Greece and Libya to the westward; but because the trade on the Red Sea was more profitable, the Tyrians conducted it in partnership with Solomon <gloss>(i)</gloss> and the other Kings of Judah, until after the Trojan War: likewise did the inhabitants of Aradus, Arvad, or Arpad; for in the Persian Gulf there were two islands <gloss>(k)</gloss> named Aradus and Tyre, where there were temples like those of Phoenicia: The Tyrians and Aradians then sailed this far and further to the coasts of India, while the Sidonians visited the Mediterranean Sea; and for this reason, Homer so exalts Sidon, and does not even mention Tyre. This departure of the Tyrians from the Red Sea and their navigation of the Mediterranean Sea, as well as the flight of the Sidonians before David to the Philistines, gave grounds for the tradition of the ancient Persians and the Phoenicians themselves, which *Herodotus* (n) relates: that the latter originally came from the Red Sea to the coasts of the Mediterranean, and immediately undertook long voyages upon it. For the same writer says at the beginning of his first book that the Phoenicians, coming from the Red to the Mediterranean Sea and beginning long voyages with Egyptian and Assyrian merchandise, landed among other places at Argos; there, after having sold their goods, they took captive some Greek women who had come to buy them and carried them away to Egypt; among which women was Io, the daughter of Inachus. From this it appears that the Phoenicians came from the Red Sea in the days of Io and her brother Phoroneus, the King of Argos, and consequently at the time when David had conquered the Edomites and caused them to flee from the Red Sea in every direction—some into Egypt with their young King, and others to the Philistines, their nearest neighbors and David’s sworn enemies. This flight was also what gave the Philistines the opportunity to name various places Erythra, in memory of the fact that they were Erythraeans or Edomites <note>The name "Edom" in Hebrew means "Red," which translates to "Erythros" in Greek. The Kingdom of the Macedonians *(i)* was founded by Caranus and Perdiccas, who, being of the royal house of Temenus, King of Argos, fled from there during the reign of Phidon, the brother of Caranus. Temenus was one of the three brothers who led the Heraclidae <note>The "Heraclidae" were the descendants of the hero Hercules who returned to the Peloponnese to reclaim their ancestral lands.</note> into the Peloponnese and divided that region among themselves: Argos fell to his lot; and after him and his son Ceisus, that kingdom was divided among their descendants until Phidon reunited it and drove out his relatives. Phidon became powerful through this; introduced measures, weights, and the minting of silver money in the Peloponnese; and, after he had pushed the Elians and Spartans aside, presided over the Olympic games: but was defeated shortly thereafter by the Elians and Spartans. *Herodotus (k)* considers Perdiccas the first King of Macedonia; later writers such as *Livy, Pausanias,* and *Suidas* have Caranus reign first; *Justin* calls Perdiccas the successor of Caranus; and *Solinus* says that Caranus was followed by Perdiccas, and that the latter first obtained the name of King. It is probable that Caranus and Perdiccas were contemporaries in government, that they fled from Phidon at the same time and initially established small lordships in Macedonia, which were united under Perdiccas after Caranus’s death. *Herodotus (a)* also says that Areus or Argaeus, Philip, Aeropus, Alcetas, Amyntas, and Alex-

->### OF THE GREEKS.<-

Alexander, after Perdiccas, reigned in a steady succession. Alexander <note>Alexander I of Macedon, known as "The Philhellene."</note> was a contemporary of Xerxes, King of Persia, died in the fourth year of the seventy-ninth Olympiad, and was succeeded by Perdiccas, just as he was by his son Archelaus: and *Thucydides (b)* tells us that before this Archelaus, eight kings reigned in Macedonia. The chronologists have assigned more than 40 years of reign to each of these kings, thereby making Phidon and Caranus live before the beginning of the Olympiads; but if one assigns to each prince 18 or 20 years of reign, and then counts the years of the first seven reigns backward from Alexander's death, then the reign of Phidon, and the founding of the Kingdom of Macedonia under Caranus and Perdiccas, will fall around the forty-sixth or forty-seventh Olympiad or thereabouts. This could scarcely have occurred earlier; for Leocides, the son of Phidon, and Megacles, the son of Alcmaeon, courted at the same time Agarista, the daughter of Cleisthenes King of Sicyon, as *Herodotus (c)* testifies; and the Amphictyons <note>An ancient religious association of Greek tribes.</note> appointed, on the advice of Solon, Alcmaeon, Cleisthenes, and Eurolycus King of Thessaly as generals of their army in the war against the Cirrheans, during which Cirrha was taken in the second year of the forty-seventh Olympiad, as the aforementioned marble stones <note>The Arundel Marbles, also known as the Parian Chronicle, an ancient Greek inscription recording dates of historical and legendary events.</note> state. So that Phidon and his brother Caranus were contemporaries of Solon, Alcmaeon, Cleisthenes, and Eurolycus; and these flourished around the 48th and 49th Olympiads. That they were also contemporaries of Croesus in their old age is evident from the fact that Solon associated with Croesus, and that Alcmaeon entertained the envoys whom Croesus sent to Delphi in the first year of the 56th Olympiad to consult the oracle, as the Arundel Marbles say; for which Croesus summoned him to his court and rewarded him with great riches.

# OF ANTIQUITIES

<meta>catchword: alli-</meta>

If we consider the reigns of Kings to be of the same length as generations, and set three generations within 100 years, one must reduce the duration of the reigns of these Princes, on average, from a ratio of seven to four. Thus, the chronology we find on the marble stones <note>The Parian Chronicle, an ancient Greek timeline inscribed on marble.</note> for the conquest of Media by Cyrus, in the fourth year of the 60th Olympiad, will come much closer to the truth through the aforementioned reduction. The marble stones say that the Cirrheans <note>Inhabitants of the city of Cirrha, central to the First Sacred War.</note> in the second year of the 47th Olympiad—which is 54 years before the conquest of Media—were defeated by the Amphictyons <note>An association of Greek neighboring tribes.</note>; and these years, being reduced by a ratio of 4 to 7, leave 31 years, which, when counted back from the fourth year of the 60th Olympiad, places the capture of Cirrhea in the first year of the 53rd Olympiad. According to a similar correction of the marble stones, Alcmaeon entertained the envoys of Croesus <note>The famously wealthy King of Lydia.</note> in the first year of the 53rd Olympiad—that is, four years before Sardis was taken by Cyrus—and the tyranny of Pisistratus in Athens, which they place in the fourth year of the 54th Olympiad, actually began in the third year of the 57th Olympiad; and Solon died, consequently, one year later. However, one should only take this path if other proofs are lacking; as long as they are available, there is no necessity for this method.

Iphitus <margin>(d)</margin> <note>A legendary King of Elis who restored the Olympic Games.</note> held the presidency in the temple of Olympian Jupiter <note>original: "Jupiter Olympus"</note> and over the Olympic games, as did his successors until the 26th Olympiad, and until that time the victors were rewarded with a <margin>(*)</margin> tripod: but the Pisans <note>The people of Pisa, an ancient town in the Peloponnese that vied for control of the Olympics.</note>, gaining the upper hand over the Eleans at that time, began to preside, presented the victors with a crown, instituted the games called *Carnea* for Apollo, and held the presidency until Phidon disturbed them in it—that is, until about the 49th Olympiad: for in the 48th <margin>(e)</margin> Olympiad, the Eleans, suspecting the intentions of the Pisans, invaded their land; but were forced to return quickly: the Pisans alli- <note>The Dutch catchword "verbon-" (allied) indicates the sentence continues on the next page.</note>

In my view, it was during this war that Phidon presided over the Olympic Games, likely in the 49th Olympiad; for in the 50th *(f)* <note>original: "f"; Ibid. [referring to Pausanias] book 5, chapter 9.</note> Olympiad, to end the disputes among the Kings over the presidency, two men from the city of Elis were chosen by lot for that purpose. The number of these was increased to nine in the 65th Olympiad, and later to ten; and these judges were called *Hellenodicae*, that is, <term>Judges for or in the name of Greece</term>. *Pausanias* relates that the Eleans called upon Phidon in the 8th Olympiad and celebrated the games with him; but he should have placed this in the 49th Olympiad. And although *Herodotus* says that Phidon pushed the Eleans "behind the bench" <note>An idiom meaning to set aside, marginalize, or remove from their rightful position.</note>, both accounts may nonetheless be true: suppose that the Eleans called upon Phidon for help against the Pisans; that after their common victory, they were excluded from the presidency by him; and that they then allied themselves with the Spartans, and with their assistance, overcame the Kingdom of Phidon, thus recovering their ancient right of presidency.

*Strabo (g)* <note>original: "g"; book 8, page 358.</note> says that Phidon was the tenth descendant of Temenus; not the tenth King, for between Kisus, the son of Temenus, and Phidon, there were no Kings of Argos; so that he descended in the tenth generation from Temenus, the latter being included. These nine intervals through the eldest sons, calculated at 27 years each, result in 243 years; and these, being counted back from the 48th Olympiad in which Phidon flourished, place the <term>Return of the Heraclidae</term> <note>The legendary event where the descendants of Hercules returned to claim their ancestral lands in the Peloponnese, used as a foundational date in Greek history.</note> approximately 50 years before the beginning of the Olympiads, as we mentioned above. However, the ancient chronologists calculate some 515 years from the return of the Heraclidae to the 48th Olympiad, and count Phidon as the seventh after Temenus, whereby they allow 85 years for every generation—a chronology that is not to be followed.

When the Greeks and Latins established their complex chronology <gloss>(i)</gloss> there were great disagreements concerning the age of Rome: the Greeks traced it back to before the Olympiads <note>The four-year cycles used in Greek dating, starting traditionally in 776 BCE</note>: some said that Aeneas had built that city; some attributed that honor to Romus, the son or grandson of Aeneas; some to Romus the son or grandson of Latinus, King of the Aborigines; and others to Romus, the son of Ulysses, Ascanius, or Italus: some of the Latins initially leaned toward the opinion of those Greeks who said that Romeus, the son or grandson of Aeneas, founded Rome. *Timaeus* of Sicily embraced this latter view, and placed the time of its construction more than a hundred years before the Olympiads: the same was done by *Naevius* the poet, who lived 20 years before *Ennius*, served in the First Punic War, and wrote a history of it. Erechtheus, then, followed immediately after Cranaus, while Amphictyon ruled at Thermopylae. *Herodotus* (q) says that the Phoenicians, who came to Greece with Cadmus, brought various kinds of learning there; for among those Phoenicians was a band of people called *Curetes*, who were practiced above others in the arts and sciences of Phoenicia; some of them settled (r) in Phrygia, where they were called Corybantes; some in Crete, where they were named Idaean Dactyli; some in Rhodes, where they received the name of Telchines; some in Samothrace, where they assumed the name of Cabiri; some in Euboea, where, before the invention of iron, they worked in copper in a city called Chalcis <note>The name Chalcis is derived from the Greek word *chalkos*, meaning copper or bronze</note>; some in Lemnos, where they assisted Vulcan; and some in Imbros and other places: but they occupied Aetolia above all other regions, and moved there in such great numbers that the region acquired the name "the land of the Curetes"; until Aetolus, the son of Endymion, having defeated Apis, the King of Sicyon, fled here and, with the assistance of his father, attacked the Curetes and, after seizing the land, named it Aetolia after his own name. With the help of the aforementioned craftsmen, Cadmus found gold in Mount Pangaeus in Thrace, and copper near Thebes; and because of this discovery, copper ore is still called *Kadmia* <note>original: "Kadmia"; now known as calamine or zinc ore, which was historically found alongside copper and used to make brass</note> today. In all the places where the Curetes settled, they first worked in copper; but when they had found iron, they moved on to the working of it: and after they had made themselves weapons and armor, they danced in them around the sacrifices with great bustle and noise, with bells, pipes, drums, and swords; and on days of music, they struck each other’s weapons with the latter, appearing, as it were, to be possessed by a divine frenzy; and the origin of music in Greece is attributed to the noise of their weapons. Thus says *Solinus* (s): <note>original Latin: "Studium musicum inde caeptum cum Idaei Dactyli modulos crepitu & tinnitu aeris deprehensos in versificum ordinem transtulissent."</note> "The study of music began there, when the Idaean Dactyli translated the rhythms captured from the clatter and tinkling of bronze into a poetic meter."
