# ->OF ANTIQUITY<-

"...the Priests, named the Idaean Dactyli <note>Legendary ancient craftsmen and healers associated with Mount Ida</note>, who brought the sounds, invented on their copper shields, to a poetic rhythm." And *Isidore (t)*, *The study of music was begun by the Idaean Dactyli* <note>original: "Studium musicum ad Idaeis Dactylis caeptum"</note>. That is: "The love of music originates from the Idaean Dactyli." But Apollo and the Muses lived only two generations after this.

*Clement (u)* calls the Idaean Dactyli barbarians—that is, foreigners—and says they were regarded as the first wise men, to whom both the invention of letters, called Ephesian <note>Ephesian letters (Ephesia Grammata) were ancient Greek magical formulas or a primitive script associated with the goddess Artemis</note>, and the introduction of musical rhymes are attributed. It appears that when the Phoenician letters, which are attributed to Cadmus, were first brought into Greece, they were at the same time carried by the Curetes into Phrygia and Crete; and that they gave them the name of Ephesian letters, after the city of Ephesus where they were first taught. Because the Curetes worked in copper and iron, and made from them swords, weapons, and sharp tools for the felling and working of wood, they introduced a new way of fighting into Europe; and gave the beginning to the crafts of smiths and carpenters, which are the primary trades for the building of ships.

Minos also made very good use of this by equipping a fleet with which he gained dominion over the seas: this *(v)* fleet of Minos was, however, without sails; but when Daedalus fled from him, he fashioned sails upon his ship. From this it appears that the Greeks used no ships with sails before the flight of Daedalus and the death of Minos, who was slain when he pursued Daedalus to Sicily during the reign of Rehoboam <note>A biblical king of Judah, son of Solomon, used here to synchronize Greek myth with biblical chronology</note>. In the latter part of the reign of Solomon, Daedalus and his nephew Talus invented the use of the adze, the saw, the drill, the plumb-line, the compass, the turner's lathe, glue, and the potter's wheel: Daedalus's father, named Eupalemus, had already previously invented the anchor: and through this, various crafts and trades in Europe had their beginning.

# ->OF THE GREEKS<-

The ($w$) Curetes <note>Ancient priests and armored dancers associated with the goddess Rhea</note> who, as we have seen, introduced letters, music, poetry, dancing, and other arts, and were present at the sacrifices, were no less active in bringing religious institutions into practice. Due to their knowledge and experience in secret arts, they were held by the common people to be not only wise men but also sorcerers. In Phrygia, they taught the mysteries of Rhea, otherwise named the Mother of the Gods, or—depending on the places where she was honored—Cybele, Berecynthia, Pessinuntia, Dindymene, Mygdonia, and the Idaean Phrygia. In Crete and Aetolia, they taught those of Jupiter Olympius <note>The Greek god Zeus</note>, the son of the Cretan Rhea. Of him they said that, when ($x$) he was born in Crete, his mother Rhea had him raised in a cave of Mount Ida under their care and supervision; that they danced around him in their armor ($y$) and with great noise, so that his father Saturn <note>The Titan Cronus</note> would not hear his crying; that they assisted him, when he had grown up, in overcoming his father and his father's friends; and that they had instituted their mysteries in memory of these things. *Bochart* ($z$) <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant scholar who sought to trace Greek myths back to Phoenician and Hebrew origins</note> believes that they came from Palestine and derived their name Curetes from the Cherethites or Cheretim, a people among the Philistines (*1 Samuel 30:14, Ezekiel 25:16, and Zephaniah 2:5*); for the Philistines seized Sidon and mingled with the Sidonians.

The first two Kings of Crete, after the landing of the Curetes on that island, were Asterius and Minos. Europa was the wife of Asterius and mother of Minos; and the Idaean Curetes were her countrymen, who came to Crete with her brother Atymnus. During her reign, they lived in a cave on Mount Ida, where they raised Jupiter, discovered iron, and manufactured weaponry. From this it appears that these three persons—Asterius, Europa, and Minos—must be the Saturn, the Rhea, and the Jupiter of the Cretans. It is true—

Because Saturn taught the Italians the use of letters, the minting of money, agriculture, various crafts, and the building of cities, one can see that he fled from Crete after letters, minting, and crafts were brought into Europe by the Phoenicians; and from Attica after Ceres had instructed the Greeks in agriculture; and thus he could not be older than Asterius, Europa, and her brother Cadmus. Italy was, according to <term>Tertullian</term> <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was an early Christian author who argued that the pagan gods were merely ancient kings who had been deified after death.</note>, first called Oenotria and then Saturnia, and from this it appears that Saturn arrived in that region after Oenotrus, so that he did not live before the sons of Lycaon. Oenotrus led the first Greek colony into Italy, Saturn the second, and Evander the third; and the Latins knew no events of their land before the times of Janus and Saturn. Jasion was the brother of Dardanus, married Cybele the daughter of Maion, King of Phrygia, and with her fathered Corybas: when he died, Dardanus, Cybele, and Corybas traveled to Phrygia and brought the mysteries of the Mother of the Gods there; and Cybele named that Goddess after her own name, just as Corybas gave the name of Corybantes to her priests. In this manner *Diodorus* [b] relates it; but *Dionysius* says that Dardanus established the Samothracian mysteries after his wife Chryse had learned them in Arcadia, and that Idaeus, the son of Dardanus, later brought the mysteries of the Mother of the Gods to Phrygia. The Phrygian Gods, like the Phoenician Astarte, were depicted on a chariot pulled by lions, with a turreted crown <note>A crown shaped like city walls, typically worn by the goddess Cybele as a protector of cities.</note> on her head, and with a drum in her hand; and the Corybantes danced around her sacrifices with a frenzied noise, just as the Idaean Dactyls did for those of Jupiter. *Lucian* [c], speaking of this Goddess, testifies that she was the Cretan Rhea—that is, Europa, the mother of Minos. Thus the Phoenicians introduced the practice of deifying dead men and women among the Greeks and Phrygians; for I find no example of this in Greece before the arrival of Cadmus and Europa from Sidon.

From these beginnings, it became common practice among the Greeks to celebrate the funeral rites of their deceased elders with festivals, invocations, and offerings for their departed souls; and for persons of famous virtue or bravery, they established magnificent burial places or rather temples, with altars and statues; wherein they publicly, through offerhan- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "offerhan-", likely leading to "offerhanden" (sacrificial offerings) on the following page.</note>

This deification of the deceased occurred in various ways, according to the qualities, circumstances, and merits of the individuals. Some were served only within private households as *Dii Penates* <note>original Latin: "Dii Penates" — Roman household deities who protected the home and its stores.</note> or Household Gods; the memory of others was honored through public tombstones upon which annual sacrifices were lit. For some, burial places were built in the form of houses or temples; for others, mysteries and ceremonies were established, and for these, sacrifices, feast days, and societies were also ordained, as well as an order of priests to perform those institutions in the temples and teach them to posterity. ...the son <note>Deucalion, the son of Prometheus, is traditionally credited with the post-flood repopulation of Greece and the establishment of religious rites.</note> of Prometheus brought the twelve Thracian Gods to Greece. **Herodotus (e)** says that these Gods came from Egypt, and from the names of various Egyptian cities that were dedicated to these Gods, it is certain that they were of Egyptian origin. The Egyptians themselves said, according to **Diodorus, (f)** that after their Saturn and Rhea, Jupiter and Juno—the father and mother of Osiris and Isis, and the grandfather and grandmother of Horus and Bastet—reigned.

Just as the Egyptians deified their deceased Kings and began the chronology of their monarchy with the reigns of their Gods and Heroes, saying that Menes was the first of the men who ruled after the Gods; so too did the Cretans have their "ages" which they attributed to their Gods and Heroes. They named the first four ages of their deified Kings and Princes the Golden, Silver, Bronze <note>Original: "kopere," literally copper, but referring to the mythological Bronze Age.</note>, and Iron Ages. **Hesiod (g)**, describing these four ages of the Gods and Demigods of the Greeks, depicts them as four human generations, each of which ended when those living at the time grew old and descended to the grave. He says that the fourth age ended with the wars of Thebes and Troy; and from the arrival of the Phoenicians and Curetes <note>The Curetes were legendary armed priests or guardians associated with the infant Zeus on Crete.</note> with Cadmus and Europa in Greece, until the destruction of Troy, there were exactly four generations. **Apollonius of Rhodes (h)** relates that when the Argonauts arrived in Crete, they slew Talus, a bronze man who had remained from the Bronze Age. Now, Talus was held to be a son of Minos, so that his offspring lived in the Bronze Age, while he himself ruled in the Silver. It was then in the Silver Age that the Greeks began to plow their land and sow corn; for Ceres <note>The Roman name for Demeter, the goddess of agriculture.</note>, who taught them this, flourished in the days of Celeus, Erechtheus, and Minos. # OF ANTIQUITIES

[The] Kings of Argos and Sicyon presented several contemporary rulers of Argos as if they reigned sequentially, and included many embellished names in the list of Sicyonian kings.

Inachus had several sons who ruled in various regions of the Peloponnese <note>The peninsula forming the southern part of Greece</note>, where they built cities or hamlets. Thus, Phoroneus founded Phoronicum, which was later named Argos after his grandson Argus; Aegialeus founded Aegialea, which was afterward named Sicyon after Sicyon, the grandson of Erechtheus; and Phegeus founded Phegea, which later took the name of Psophis from the daughter of Lycaon. These three cities were the oldest in the Peloponnese. After them, Sisyphus—the son of Aeolus and grandson of Hellen <note>original: "Helenus"; likely referring to Hellen, the mythological progenitor of the Greeks</note>—built Ephyra, which was later called Corinth; and Aethlius, the son of Aeolus, founded Elis. Before Phoroneus, Cecrops had already built the fortress of Athens, called Cecropia; and Lycaon had built Lycosura, considered by some to be the oldest city in Arcadia. The sons of the latter, who numbered at least twenty-four, each built a city for themselves—except for Oenotrus, their youngest brother, who only grew up after his father's death and sailed with his people to Italy. There, he taught the inhabitants how to build cities and became the Janus <note>The Roman god of beginnings and transitions, here identified with a historical migrant</note> of the Latins. Phoroneus also had several sons and grandsons who ruled in various regions and founded cities there, such as Kar, Apis, and others; and Haemon, the son of Pelasgus, settled in Haemonia, afterward called Thessaly, where he followed his contemporaries in the building of cities.

Because of these divisions and subdivisions of the states of the first Greek princes, the history of the early kingdoms of the Peloponnese has become uncommonly confused. This gave the Greeks the opportunity, out of vain glory, to claim these states were much older than they truly were. However, according to the various chronologies established previously, it is certain that the first civilization of the Greeks—their living in houses and neighborhoods and the building of the oldest cities in Europe—could have begun barely more than two or three generations before Cadmus of Sidon <note>A Phoenician prince credited with bringing the alphabet to Greece</note> arrived in Greece. It is probable that this [civilization] was caused by the expulsion of the shepherds <note>A reference to the Hyksos, or "Shepherd Kings," who were expelled from Egypt and whose migrations are often linked by early modern historians to the founding of Greek colonies</note>.

### OF THE GREEKS.

[...travelers] from Egypt in the days of Eli and Samuel; as a result, they were forced to seek other dwelling places in Greece in great numbers. But it is very difficult to arrange the genealogy and chronology of the Greek "fable-ages" <note>The mythical or legendary eras of ancient history</note> into a proper order; and for this reason, I leave these matters to the further investigation of others.

Before the Phoenicians introduced the deification <term>vergooding: the practice of treating deceased humans as gods</term> of the dead, the Greeks had in every city a council of elders to whom the care of government was entrusted; as well as a certain place where these elders met, and where the people served their Gods with sacrifices. And when several of these cities placed themselves under the management of a common council for their safety, they established in one of the cities a *Prytaneum* <note>original: "Prytaneum"; a public hall in Ancient Greece housing the community's sacred hearth</note> or court, where the people gathered at set times to deliberate on their common safety and to honor the common God with sacrifices, as well as to buy and sell. The cities in which these meetings were held were called *deemoi* <note>original: "deemoi" (δῆμοι); the root of "democracy," referring to rural districts or village communities</note>, which means peoples, communities, or hamlets. And when, in the course of time, several of these *deemoi* placed themselves under the authority of a common council by mutual consent, they built a court or *prytaneum* in one of those *deemoi*, where the people gathered, deliberated, sacrificed, celebrated their festivals, and bought and sold; and such a *deemoi* they fortified with walls to be safer, and then called it *polin* <note>original: "polin" (πόλιν); the Greek word for city-state</note>, that is, the city. I take this to be the origin of the villages, hamlets, cities, common council meetings, fire-temples, feast days, and annual markets in Europe. The *prytaneum* or *pros tameion* <note>original: "pros tameion"; likely a Greek-derived phrase meaning "for the treasury" or place of storage</note> was a kind of court, provided with a place of religious worship, in which an everlasting fire was kept burning on the altar for the lighting of sacrifices. From the word *Estia* <note>original: "Estia" (Ἑστία); the Greek goddess of the hearth</note> or fire came the name *Vesta*, whom the people finally transformed into a Goddess, whereby they became like the ancient Persians in the worship of fire. When the aforementioned common assemblies decided on a war against their neighbors, they appointed a general commander over their bands, who subsequently became their King.

Thus *Thucydides* tells us: (*i*) "Attica was, under Cecrops and his descendants until Theseus, populated by a great number of cities, which all had their own particular authorities and *prytanea* <note>original: "prytanea"; the central council halls and public hearths that served as the religious and political heart of ancient Greek communities</note>: never did they seek counsel from the King unless there was a fear of danger, but every city governed its own commonwealth and had its own council; indeed, they sometimes even waged war against the Princes, as the Eleusinians, with Eumolpus, did against Erechtheus. But when Theseus, a prudent and powerful Prince, obtained the crown, he abolished the authorities and courts of the individual cities and caused them all to assemble in one court and one common council at Athens." *Polemon*, as he is cited by (*k*) *Strabo*, testifies "that one counted 170 *demes* <note>original: "deemoi" (δῆμοι); the rural districts or townships of ancient Attica</note> in the vicinity of Attica, among which was Eleusis"; and (*l*) *Philochorus* relates, "that when Attica was attacked by the Carians and Boeotians by sea and by land, Cecrops was the first who gathered the multitude (understand here the 170 *demes*) into twelve cities; that the names of those cities were Cecropia, Tetrapolis, Epacria, Decelea, Eleusis, Aphidna, Thoricus, Brauron, Cytherus, Sphettus, Cephissia, and Phalerum; and that Theseus later drew these twelve cities together into the single city of Athens."

The Kingdom of the Argives <note>The people of Argos, a powerful city-state in the Peloponnese</note> had its origin in almost the same manner; for *Pausanias* (*m*) tells us, "that Phoroneus, the son of Inachus, first gathered the Argives, who originally lived scattered and apart, into a single community; and that the city where they first assembled received the name Phoronicum, that is, the city of Phoroneus"; and *Strabo* (*n*) makes this observation, "that Homer calls all the places of the Peloponnese—a few excepted—not cities but landscapes, since each of them consisted of a confluence of several *demes* or free hamlets <term>vlekken: an old Dutch term for small, unfortified settlements or market towns, similar to villages</term>, from which noble cities later arose and were built: thus the Argives composed Mantinea in Arcadia from five, and Tegea from nine hamlets: and that Cleombrotus or Cleonymus [gathered] five hamlets within the..."

*Pausanias* (o) further testifies that the Arcadians <note>The inhabitants of Arcadia, a rugged mountainous region of the Peloponnese</note> held Pelasgus to be the first man, and that he was indeed their first King, who taught them, while they were still wild, how one builds houses to protect oneself against heat, cold, and rain; how one could prepare animal skins into clothing; and that instead of plants and roots, which were often harmful, one should eat the acorns of the beech tree <note>In Greek myth, the eating of acorns was a mark of the earliest "Pelasgian" humans before the gift of grain from Demeter</note>. It appears from this that the Greeks only began the building of houses and villages in the days of Pelasgus (the father of Lycaon) and of Lelex (the father of Myles), and consequently only two or three generations before the flood of Deucalion and the arrival of Cadmus in Europe. Until then, they lived (p) in forests and caves under the earth; and the first houses they built were only of clay, until the brothers Euryalus and Hyperbius taught them to harden the clay and build with stone. It was in the days of Ogyges, Pelasgus, Ezeus, Inachus, and Lelex, when the people, being instructed by Doxius the son of Coelus, turned their hand to the building of clay houses and villages; and during the lives of Lycaon, Phoroneus, Aegialeus, Phegeus, Eurotas, Myles, Polycaon, Cecrops, and their sons, the villages gathered themselves into *demes* <gloss>deemoi</gloss>, and those *demes* subsequently transformed into cities.

When Oenotrus, the son of Lycaon, came with a colony from Greece into Italy, (q) "he found that region mostly uninhabited, and where it was inhabited, it was very sparsely populated; so that he seized a part of it and built small but many villages in the mountains." These villages were un-walled hamlets; but when the Greek colony became numerous and dwelling places began to be lacking, "they drove the Sicels <note>original: "Sikulen"; an ancient people who inhabited Italy before migrating to Sicily</note> out of Italy, surrounded many cities with [walls]"

## CHAPTER II.

->*Of the Antiquities of the Egyptians.*<-

The Egyptians boasted in ancient times of their great and long-lasting monarchy under the Kings Ammon, Osiris, Bacchus, Sesostris, Hercules, Memnon, and others; according to their claims, their borders extended eastward as far as India and westward to the Atlantic Sea; and out of a vain arrogance, they made their reign several thousand years older than the creation of the world. Let us therefore attempt to improve the Egyptian chronology by comparing the affairs of Egypt with those of the contemporary Greeks and Hebrews.

Bacchus, the conqueror, loved two women named Venus and Ariadne: Venus was the mistress of Anchises and Cinyras, and the mother of Aeneas. All these persons lived until the destruction of Troy, and the sons of Bacchus and Ariadne were among the Argonauts <note>The Argonauts were the legendary heroes who accompanied Jason in his quest for the Golden Fleece</note>, as we have shown above; so that the great Bacchus flourished only one generation before the expedition of the Argonauts. This Prince <margin>[a] See Hermippus, as cited in Athenaeus, Book 1.</margin> was powerful at sea, brought his victorious weapons as far as India, returned in triumph, and led his army across the Hellespont <note>The Dardanelles, the narrow strait in northwestern Turkey connecting the Aegean Sea to the Sea of Marmara</note>; then he took possession of Thrace and introduced music, dancing, and poetry there; he defeated Lycurgus, King of Thrace, and Pentheus, the grandson of Cadmus; he gave the Kingdom of Lycurgus to Tharops, and one of his singers or players, called Calliope by the Greeks, to Oeagrus, the son of Tharops; and from this pair was born Orpheus, who sailed with the Argonauts. This Bacchus was then a contemporary of Sesostris <note>A legendary King of Egypt often identified with the historical Pharaohs Senusret III or Ramses II</note>; and since both are described as Kings of Egypt, as powerful at sea, as great conquerors, and as having carried their conquests as far as India and Thrace—

The ancient Greeks, who embellished the fables of the Gods, recount that Io, the daughter of Inachus, was led away to Egypt and there became the Egyptian Isis; and that Apis, the son of Phoroneus <note>Phoroneus was a legendary king of Argos, often cited as one of the first men in Greek mythology</note>, was regarded as the God Serapis after his death; and some also say that Epaphus was a son of Io. Now, Serapis and Epaphus are the same as Osiris; so that Isis and Osiris, according to the opinion of the ancient Greeks (who embellished the fables of the Gods), were no more than two or three generations older than the expedition of the Argonauts. Dicaearchus, as he is cited by the scholiast <note>A "scholiast" is an ancient commentator who wrote explanatory notes (scholia) in the margins of classical manuscripts</note> on Apollonius, <margin>(b) Argonautica, Book 4, line 272.</margin> presents them as being two generations older than Sesostris, saying that Sesonchosis reigned after the death of Horus, the son of Osiris and Isis. He seems to have followed the opinion of the people of Naxos, which made Bacchus two generations older than Theseus, and for that purpose invented two Minoses and two Ariadnes; for according to the consensus of all antiquity, Osiris and Bacchus were one and the same King of Egypt. This was testified by both the Egyptians and the Greeks; and some of the ancient mythologists, such as Eumolpus and Orpheus, called Osiris <margin>(c) Diodorus Siculus, Book 1, page 7.</margin> by the names of Dionysus and Sirius. Osiris was King over all Egypt and a great conqueror; in the days of Triptolemus he crossed the Hellespont, conquered Thrace, and there defeated Lycurgus; so that his undertaking corresponds with that of the great Bacchus. Now, Osiris, Bacchus, and Sesostris <note>Sesostris is a legendary king of Egypt mentioned by Herodotus, often identified with the historical Pharaoh Senusret or Ramesses II</note> lived at approximately the same time and were, according to the account of the historians, all Kings of Egypt who ruled at Thebes, adorned that city, and were very powerful at sea and on land: all three were great conquerors who extended their conquests by land through Asia as far as India: all three crossed the Hellespont and were in danger of losing their army there: all three took possession of Thrace, set a limit to their victories there, and returned from there to Egypt.

Having conquered everything, he easily established cities and appeared to be completely invincible. At that time, the coastal region from Sidon to the borders of Egypt was all called Phoenicia. One king had been set over it in ancient times, as is agreed by all who have recorded the oldest history of the Phoenicians. The luni-solar year that had been used by Noah and all his descendants, and which, according to a calendar or almanac, consisted of twelve months, each of thirty days, was also observed by them until this time; but now they added five days to it to make the length of the year equal with the course of the sun.

The ancient Egyptians embellished a story, <gloss>(k)</gloss> that Rhea lay secretly with Saturn, and having been made pregnant by him, she prayed to Sol <note>original: "Sol," the Latin name for the Sun god, likely referring here to Ra.</note> that she might not give birth to her fruit in any of the months of the year; that Mercury and Luna <note>original: "Luna," the Latin name for the Moon.</note> then playing with dice, the former won the game, and from that he subtracted a seventy-second part of each day of the lunar year, from which he composed five days to add after the 360 others, so that Rhea might give birth on one of them; and that this was the reason why the Egyptians celebrated those five days as the birthdays of Osiris, Horus the Elder, Typhon, Isis, and Nephthys the wife of Typhon, who were all children of Rhea. From this fable of the ancient Egyptians, it appears that the five days, which the solar year is longer than the lunar year, were added to their almanac under the reign of Saturn and Rhea, the parents of Osiris, Isis, and Typhon; that is in the days of Ammon and Titea, the parents of the Titans <note>The author is synchronizing Greek and Egyptian mythology with historical figures, suggesting the "Titans" were a specific group of people living during this era.</note>; or about the twentieth year of David’s reign, when these Titans were born, and consequently shortly after the flight of the Edomites to Egypt before David: but since the time of the solstices was not yet determined, the beginning of this year was first established at the midnight of spring <note>Referring to the spring equinox.</note>, when Amenophis, the successor of Horus the Younger, who was a son of Osiris and Isis, ruled over Egypt.

It is probable that the Edomites who sought refuge in Egypt with Hadad also brought the use of letters <note>Meaning the art of alphabetic writing.</note> with them there: for these had long been in use among Abraham's descendants, who lived in Stony Arabia <note>original: "ſteenachtig Arabië," referring to Arabia Petraea.</note> and on the coast of the Red Sea, in which region Moses long before wrote the law in a book and engraved it on stone tablets. <margin>(*p*) In Photius, chapter 279. (*q*) Fable 274. (*r*) In Eusebius's *Chronicle*.</margin> Helladius (*p*) relates that a man named Oes, who appeared in the Red Sea with the tail of a fish (the Egyptians' representation of a sailor), taught astronomy and letters: *Hyginus* (*q*) says that Euhadnes, who came from the sea into Chaldea, was the first who taught the Chaldeans star-gazing <note>original: "starrekykkunde," which the author clarifies refers to astronomy.</note> (he means astronomy): and *Alexander Polyhistor* (*r*) testifies from *Berossus*, that Oannes taught the Chaldeans letters, the mathematical and other arts, agriculture, living together in cities, and the building of temples; and that several such men subsequently landed in that region. The names Oes, Euhadnes, and Oannes appear, with a small change or corruption, to be the same; and I believe that they were common to various sailors, who from time to time came here, and consequently navigated that sea for the conduct of trade, or fled across it from their enemies. This we always learn from the cited writers: that the knowledge of letters and astronomy, as well as that of agriculture and city-building, was brought into Chaldea from across the sea; that those arts and sciences were first taught by sailors who traversed the Persian Gulf from time to time, and consequently after they were already introduced among the nations from which they came; that is in the days of Ammon, Shishak, David, Solomon, and their successors, or at least not long before. The Red Sea received 그 name not because of its color, but after the names <gloss>(s)</gloss> Edom and Erythra <note>original: "Erythra," the Greek word for red, corresponding to the Hebrew "Edom."</note> which Esau bore, and which mean "red": and some <gloss>(t)</gloss> recount that Esau, whom they call King Erythra, invented the vessels with which that sea was navigated, and that he was buried on an island near the Persian Gulf. Before this time, small boats or skiffs had already been invented, with which the Patriarchs crossed the Euphrates and the Jordan—just as other nations did over many other rivers—either to seek out lands for their habitation or to plunder their neighbors. It may be that Ishmael and Midian, Abraham's sons, as well as his grandson Esau, built larger ships following the example of those small vessels, in order to seek out and inhabit the islands of the Red Sea; and subsequently practiced navigation to such an extent that they could sail along the coast of the Arabian Sea as far as the Persian Gulf: for the use of ships, even on the Mediterranean Sea, seems to have been already known in <gloss>(u)</gloss> Jacob's days, certainly in those of the <gloss>(v)</gloss> Judges; although it is likely that the merchants who navigated the Red Sea were not diligent in continuing or teaching others the arts and sciences upon which their commerce and navigation rested. 

The most probable view, then, is that the arts of letters, mathematics, astronomy, and architecture were first invented by the merchants who lived near the Red Sea, in order to record their merchandise, to settle their accounts, to be able to trust in the guidance of the stars by night, and to build ships for the transport of their goods: and that those arts, at the time when David conquered the land of these merchants and scattered them, [spread] out of stony Arabia <note>referring to Arabia Petraea</note> to Egypt, Chaldea,

Under Tabrimmon’s reign, Shishak <note>original: "Sifak"; the author uses the Dutch rendering of the Pharaoh Shishak (Sheshonq I), who plundered Jerusalem.</note> conquered Syria and subjected it to the Egyptian domain; and after it had regained its freedom under Ben-Hadad I, it became subject to the kingdom of Israel in the days of Ben-Hadad III until the reign of Rezin; but in the ninth year of Hoshea, the King of Israel, Tiglath-Pileser the King of Assyria marched against Syria, took those people captive, killed Rezin, and consequently brought their rule to an end. *Josephus* <margin>(d) Antiquities, book 9, ch. 2.</margin> now relates that the Syrians, until "into his own days, worshiped the gods Adar—that is, Hadad or Ben-Hadad—and his successor Hazael, both because of the benefits provided to their subjects and because they had adorned the city of Damascus with temples; and daily," continues *Josephus*, "they celebrate ceremonies in honor of these Kings, and boast of their great antiquity; not knowing that they are from recent times, and that no more than eleven hundred years have passed since they lived." It seems that these Kings had built magnificent burial places for themselves, and that they were worshiped therein after their death. *Justin* <margin>(e) book 36.</margin> <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a 2nd-century Roman historian.</note> calls the first of these princes Damascus, and says, "that the city of Damascus received its name after him, and that the Syrians, out of respect for him, worshiped his wife Arathis as a goddess, using her burial place as a temple."

Byblos, the origin of which I shall unfold at length. When Rhadamanthus [f] the brother of the Cretan King Minos, under his reign, led various colonies from Crete to the Greek Islands and entrusted their rule to his military commanders, he gave, among others, the island of Lemnos to Thoas—also called Theias or Thoantes—the father of Hypsipyle. This Thoas was a Cretan craftsman in metals, and consequently a pupil of the Idaean Dactyls <note>The Idaean Dactyls were mythical metalworkers and magicians said to have discovered iron on Mount Ida; the author views them as historical teachers of craft.</note>, and was perhaps a Phoenician; for the Idaean Dactyls, as well as the Telchines and Corybantes <note>Ancient groups of priests or metalworkers associated with the mysteries of Crete and Rhodes.</note>, had come with their arts and sciences from Phoenicia to Crete and Greece. *Suidas* [g] says of this Thoas that he was a descendant of Pharnaces, King of Cyprus; *Apollodorus* testifies [h] that he had Sandochus, a Syrian, as his father; and *Apollonius of Rhodes* [i] relates,

"that Hypsipyle gave a purple cloak to Jason, which
"cloak the Graces had fashioned for Bacchus, and which
"had been given by him to his son Thoas, the father of Hypsipyle and
"King of Lemnos."

This Thoas [p] married Calycopice <note>A name often associated with Aphrodite or Venus in ancient genealogies.</note>, the mother of Aeneas and daughter of Otreus, King of Phrygia; because of his skill on the harp, he received the name of Cinyras <note>Cinyras was a legendary hero-king of Cyprus; the name is linked to the Greek word 'kinyra,' a type of lyre or harp.</note>; and he was exceedingly beloved by Apollo or Horus, the son of Shishak <note>The author equates the Egyptian Pharaoh Shishak (Sheshonq I) with the gods of mythology, a common practice in 18th-century historical chronologies.</note>. Catching the great Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note> consorting with his wife in Phrygia, where they lay together in bed, Bacchus pacified him for this with wine and, to cover his shame with a crown, elevated him to be King of Byblos and Cyprus; after which he crossed the Hellespont and took possession of Thrace. On these matters the poets played in their fables: "that Vulcan 
"fell down from heaven onto the island of Lemnos, that Bacchus 
"pacified him with wine [q], and took him up into heaven 
"once more." 

Thoas "fell from the heaven" of the Cretan gods when he departed from Crete for Lemnos to work in metals, and was "taken up into it once more" when Bacchus elevated him to be King of Byblos and Cyprus. In the latter kingdom, he gathered great treasures and ruled until his old age—

The Egyptians gave the name of (*h*) *Nephthys* <note>The author connects the goddess Nephthys to the "edges" or coasts of the land, contrasting her with Isis (the fertile land).</note> to all sea coasts, headlands, and regions that stretched toward the sea and were washed by it: and *Bochart* as well as *Arias Montanus* <note>Samuel Bochart and Benito Arias Montano were influential 16th and 17th-century scholars who attempted to map biblical geography onto the ancient world.</note> places the Naphtuhim—a people descended from Mizraim (*i*), the son of Ham—on the coasts of Marmarica and Cyrene <note>Regions in modern-day Libya.</note>. This was done both to inform them of the confusion in which that empire found itself, and to urge them to throw off the Egyptian yoke, liberate themselves, and enter into a defensive alliance with the Greeks. Athothes, or Thoth, the Secretary of Osiris; Toforthrus, or Asclepius <note>original: "Eskulaap"; the Greek god of medicine and healing</note>, a physician who invented the art of building with squared stones; and Thuor, or Polybus, the husband of Alcandra, were merely Princes of Egypt. For *Sesostris* ruled in the age of the Egyptian Gods, and was himself deified under the names of Osiris, Hercules, and Bacchus <note>The Roman name for Dionysus</note>, as we have shown before; and consequently, he must be placed before Menes, Nitocris, and Moeris. Menes and his son Ramesses followed immediately after the Gods, so that Nitocris and Moeris must stand after them. In the list of Egyptian Kings by *Manetho* <note>An Egyptian priest and historian from the 3rd century BCE</note>, and in three different places in that of *Eratosthenes* <note>A Greek polymath and librarian at Alexandria</note>, Moeris is placed immediately before Cheops, and Nitocris after the builders of the three great pyramids. *Herodotus* now says that her brother reigned before her and was slain, and that she took revenge for his death; and *Syncellus* <note>A Byzantine chronicler</note> testifies that she built the third great pyramid; the Kings who built the pyramids reigned at Memphis, and consequently after Moeris. When one takes all these matters into account, I believe that the Kings of Egypt, as listed by *Herodotus*, should be placed in this order: Sesostris, Pheron, Proteus, Menes, Rhampsinitus, Moeris, Cheops, Cephren, Mykerinos, Nitocris, Asychis, Anysis, Sabacon, Anysis for the second time, Sethon, twelve simultaneous Kings <note>The Dodecarchy</note>, Psammetichus, Necho, Psammis, Apries, Amasis, and Psammenitus.

determined, they also tracked the time of the solstices <note>The two times a year when the sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky</note> through other observations, and placed the fixed stars into certain constellations; matters which all occurred under the reigns of Ammon, Shishak, Horus, and Memnon. When Nechepsos or Nikepsos <note>A legendary king of Sais often associated with early astrological texts</note> ruled at Sais, he introduced astronomy with the help of Petosiris, an Egyptian priest, basing it on the aspects of the planets and the qualities of those men or women to whom they were dedicated. When Sabacon, the King of Ethiopia, invaded Egypt with an army around the beginning of the reign of Nabonassar, the King of Babylon, a great number of Egyptians fled before him to Babylon. They introduced the reckoning of 365 days in the solar year, along with the study of astronomy and astrology, carrying these sciences with them to that place, and laid the foundation of the Era of Nabonassar <note>An astronomical calendar system starting in 747 BCE</note>. This era began with the first year of the reign of that prince, which corresponds with the 22nd year of Bochoris <note>Bakenranef, an Egyptian king of the 24th Dynasty</note>, as we noted above; and they set its commencement on the same day the Egyptian year began, so that their astronomical observations would be more convenient. *Diodorus Siculus (p)* says in this regard: "it is said that the Babylonian Chaldeans <note>The priestly class of Babylon known for their wisdom and star-gazing</note>, who originated from Egypt, were famous for their skill in astronomy, which they had learned from the priests of Egypt." And *Hestiaeus*, who wrote a history of Egypt, speaking of a heavy disaster that befell Egypt, *says (q)*: "that the Priests who survived that disaster, taking with them the sanctuaries of Jupiter Enyalius <note>original: "Jupiter Enyalius"; a reference to a war-like aspect of the deity, likely identifying a specific Egyptian temple cult moved to Babylon</note>, arrived at Shinar in Babylonia." From the 15th year of Asa <note>King of Judah</note>, in which Zerah <note>An Ethiopian commander mentioned in 2 Chronicles 14</note> was defeated and Menes or Amenophis began to reign, until the beginning of the Era of Nabonassar, 200 years elapsed. These years provide sufficient time for nine or ten royal reigns, averaging about 20 years each; and according to the account of Herodotus which we cited above, exactly that many kings reigned in that intervening time; so that his account, besides being the oldest—

that erected for *Sethon*, and seen by *Herodotus* (s), held a mouse in its hands. But among the Egyptians, a mouse was a symbol of destruction, so that the mouse in *Sethon’s* hand merely signifies that he wrought a great destruction upon the army of the Assyrians. The Scriptures tell us that when *Sennacherib*, having invaded Judea, besieged Lachish and Libnah (which occurred in the 14th year of Hezekiah’s <note>Dutch: *Hiskia*</note> reign and in the 35th of the era of Nabonassar <note>The Era of Nabonassar was a chronological system starting in 747 BCE, used by ancient astronomers and historians like Ptolemy</note>), the King of Judah then trusted in (t) Pharaoh, that is, in *Sethon* the King of Egypt; and that *Tirhaka*, the King of Ethiopia, had marched out to fight against (u) *Sennacherib*. From this account, it is probable that *Sennacherib*, having heard of the military expedition of the Kings of Egypt and Ethiopia against him, moved his army from Libnah toward Pelusium <note>A major city on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta, acting as the gateway to Egypt</note> to check their approach, and that he was surprised by them in the night and so thoroughly defeated that it was as if the bowstrings of the Assyrians had been gnawed away by mice. Some are of the opinion that the Assyrians were destroyed by lightning, or by a scorching wind <note>The *Simoom*, a dry, suffocating sandstorm common in the region, often interpreted as a divine intervention</note> that sometimes blows from the southern parts of Chaldea. After *Tirhaka* had achieved this victory, he succeeded *Sethon* in the government over Egypt, and carried his arms through Libya and Africa westward as far as the mouth of the Strait of Gibraltar. But *Herodotus* relates that the priests of Egypt reckoned *Sethon* as the last King who held dominion over Egypt before that land was divided into twelve simultaneous sovereignties <note>Known as the Dodecarchy, a period of fragmented rule before the rise of Psamtik I</note>, and consequently before the Assyrians invaded it.

For when *Esarhaddon* <note>Dutch: *Ezarhaddon*</note>, the King of Assyria, had possessed his empire for about thirteen years, he seized the Kingdom of Babylon, and transported a great multitude of people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim to the regions of Samaria and Damascus; in whose place he sent the remnant of the ten tribes of Israel and of the Syrians—who had been left in those lands by *Tiglath-Pileser*—away to Babylonia and Assyria.

Egypt was brought into subjection by Nebuchadnezzar in the second-to-last year of King Hophra <note>Hophra is the biblical name for Pharaoh Apries</note>, which is in the 178th year of the Era of Nabonassar <note>The Era of Nabonassar, beginning in 747 BCE, was a chronological system used by ancient astronomers and historians</note>: and then it remained subject to the Babylonian Empire for 40 years <margin>(a)</margin>, during the majority of the reign of Amasis, a governor to whom the care of Egypt had been entrusted by the victor. At that time, these nations regained their freedom; but three or four years later (in the year of Nabonassar 223 or 224) they were once again attacked and conquered by Cambyses <note>Cambyses II, the Persian King who integrated Egypt into the Achaemenid Empire</note>, and since then they have always remained in servitude, just as was predicted by the prophets.

The length of the reigns of Psammetichus, Necho, Psammis, Apries, Amasis, and Psammenitus, as recorded by *Herodotus*, amounts to approximately 146 and a half years in total: and just as many years passed from the 78th year of Nabonassar—when the Ethiopian dominion over Egypt came to an end—until the 224th year of the same era, in which Cambyses conquered Egypt and brought that kingdom to a close. From this, it appears that *Herodotus* was cautious and faithful in his accounts, and that he has left us a good description of the antiquities of Egypt, at least as far as the priests of Thebes, Memphis, and Heliopolis, and the Carians and Ionians living in Egypt, were able to inform him: for he consulted all of them, and both the Carians and Ionians had lived in Egypt since the time of the twelve simultaneous kings <note>A reference to the Dodecarchy mentioned on the previous page</note>.

*Pliny (b)* tells us that the Egyptian memorial columns <note>Referring here to obelisks</note> were made of a type of stone found near Syene <note>Modern-day Aswan</note> in the Thebaid; and that the first column was erected by Mitres, who reigned at Heliopolis—that is, by Mesphres, the ancestor of Misphragmuthosis <note>These names refer to Pharaohs of the 18th Dynasty, such as Thutmose III, as understood by early modern scholars</note>: and that other kings subsequently built more columns: such as Sochis, that is Sesochis.

Now, when looking at the history of Egypt since this last conquest, one finds that it was described truthfully by *Herodotus*; both regarding the number, the order, and the names of the Kings, as well as the length of their reigns. In this, he is now followed by all historians as the only one who has left us a good history of Egypt for that period. That his accounts of the earlier centuries of Egypt are less accurate is caused by the loss which the records <note>original: "gedenkfchriften"</note> of that kingdom suffered during the reigns of the Ethiopians and Assyrians; and it is without any likelihood that the priests of Egypt, who lived two or three hundred years after *Herodotus*, [knew] the history of their land...

### CHAPTER III.

->*Of the Antiquities of the Assyrians.*<-

Just as the Gods or ancient deified Kings and Princes of Greece, Egypt, and Syria or Damascus have been made much older than they truly were, so too has it gone with those of Chaldea and Assyria. ### OF THE ASSYRIANS.

“...and all your people: from the days of the Kings of Asshur <note>Assyria</note> until this day. (*Neh. IX. 31.*)” That is to say, during the time of the Assyrian Kingdom, or since the rise of that monarchy; and consequently, that monarchy began to achieve its greatness when its Princes began to oppress the inhabitants of Palestine, which occurred in the days of Pul <gloss>(b)</gloss> <note>Pul is the first Assyrian king mentioned by name in the Bible, often identified with Tiglath-Pileser III or his predecessor</note>. This King and his successors troubled Israel, and dominated the Medes and other peoples who lay around Assyria; and, upon the ruins of many small and ancient lordships, they established their monarchy. But of these conquests *Ctesias* <note>A Greek physician and historian whose accounts of Persia and Assyria were often considered legendary or exaggerated by later historians</note> knew nothing—indeed, not even the names of the victors, or that there was an Assyrian monarchy in existence at that time; for he posits that the Medes held sway during that period, and that the Kingdom of the Assyrians had already perished at least 250 years before his own timeline began.

I acknowledge, however, that Nimrod <note>A biblical figure described as a "mighty hunter" and the first king on earth</note> laid the foundation of a Kingdom at Babylon, and that it possibly extended into Assyria: but this, his Kingdom, was of a small circumference in comparison with the monarchies that appeared later. It was enclosed within the fertile fields of Chaldea, Chalonitis, and Assyria, which are washed by the rivers Tigris and Euphrates. And even if it were larger, it did not remain in that greatness for long; for it was the custom, in this youth of the world, that every father divided the regions over which he held sway among his sons. Thus Noah was first King of the whole world, Ham subsequently of all Africa, and Japheth of all Europe and Asia Minor; but these left no established lordships to their descendants. After the death of Nimrod, one finds nowhere in the Holy Scriptures mention of an Assyrian monarchy before the days of Pul. The four Kings who invaded the south of Canaan in the days of Abraham came from the regions that Nimrod <gloss>(c)</gloss> had possessed, and were possibly among his descendants, who had divided his conquered provinces among themselves. Pul or Belus <note>The author identifies the biblical Pul with the legendary Belus</note> seems to have been the first King of Assyria who extended his conquests beyond that land. Under the reign of Jeroboam <margin>(r) *Amos* 1:1, 6:2 & *Isaiah* 10:8, 9.</margin> he seized Calneh and its territory, and under that of Menahem, he invaded the borders of Israel; but he did not remain there, as Menahem <margin>(s) 2 *Kings* 15:19.</margin> ransomed himself for a thousand talents of silver. Consequently, during the reign of this Pul, the empire of the Assyrians was extended to this side of the Tigris. It appears that this Prince, who was a great warrior, subjugated Harran, Carchemish, Rezeph, Calneh, and Telassar, founded or enlarged the city of Babylon, and built the old palace that stood within its walls.

According to this testimony, she flourished four generations, or about 134 years, before Nebuchadnezzar, and consequently during the reign of Tiglath-Pileser, the successor of Pul. Shortly after the death of Phraortes, the Scythians (*k*), under the leadership of Madyes or Medus, fell upon Media and defeated the Medes in a pitched battle in the year 113 of the Era of Nabonassar <note>The Era of Nabonassar, beginning in 747 BCE, was a chronological system used by ancient astronomers like Ptolemy to date historical events accurately.</note>. After this victory, they marched from Media toward Egypt; but King Psammitichus met them as far as Phoenicia and gave them money to be spared from an invasion. Thus they returned and ruled over a great part of Asia for about 28 years. However, Cyaxares—the successor of Astyages <note>The author here reverses the traditional succession; historically, Cyaxares was the father and predecessor of Astyages. This reflects the author’s specific chronological theories.</note>—having lured several of their princes and commanders to a feast, slaughtered them with his Medes just before the destruction of Nineveh, whereupon the rest were forced to return to Scythia.

In the year 123 of the Era of Nabonassar (*l*), Nabopolassar, who commanded the armies of Chyniladon, the King of Assyria, in Chaldea, revolted against that prince and set himself up as King of Babylon. Around that time or shortly thereafter, Chyniladon was succeeded at Nineveh by the last King of Assyria, who is called Sarak in the writings of *Polyhistor*. Nebuchadnezzar, the son of Nabopolassar, subsequently married Amyite, the daughter of the Median King Astyages and sister of Cyaxares; and these two houses, being thus joined by marriage, conspired together to bring about the fall of the Assyrian monarchy. Then, Astyages having died and Nabopolassar having grown old, their sons Cyaxares and Nebuchadnezzar led the armies of Media and Babylonia against Nineveh, destroyed that city, defeated Sarak, and divided the kingdom of Assyria between themselves. The Jews attribute this victory over Nineveh to the Chaldeans, the Greeks to the Medes, and (*m*) *Tobias*, *Polyhistor*, *Josephus*, and *Ctesias* to both. The capture of this city marked the beginning of the great progress subsequently made by Nebuchadnezzar and Cyaxares, and thereby the foundation was laid for the two monarchies of the Babylonians and Medes, which were branches of the Assyrian empire. From that time on, one must reckon the fall of the empire of the Assyrians, its destroyers being then still—

### CHAPTER IV.

->*Of the Antiquities of Babylonia and Media.*<-

With the collapse of the Assyrian monarchy, the Kingdoms of Babylon and Media grew large and powerful. The years of the reigns of the Kings of Babylon were set down by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian mathematician and astronomer whose "Canon of Kings" is a primary source for ancient chronology.</note> in a list; but to understand these correctly, one must observe that the first year of every King in that list begins with the start of the last month of Thoth <note>The first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar, which "shifted" through the seasons over long periods of time; Ptolemy used it as a standard for his astronomical calculations.</note> that occurred during the reign of his predecessor. This I have determined by comparing the years of the Roman Emperors—as they are recorded in that list—with their years, months, and days as recorded by other writers. This being noted, it appears from that list that Esarhaddon <note>original: Ezarhaddon</note> died in the year 81 of the Era of Nabonassar <term>Era of Nabonassar: A chronological era beginning in 747 BCE, used by ancient astronomers to provide a continuous timeline of celestial observations.</term>, Saosduchinus <note>A Latinized name for Shamash-shum-ukin, the King of Babylon and brother of the Assyrian King Ashurbanipal.</note> in the year 101, Chyniladanus <note>original: Chyniladon; likely referring to the King Kandalanu.</note> in the year 123, Nabopolassar in the year 144, and Nebuchadnezzar in the year 187. All these Kings, along with several others named in that list, ruled one after another over Babylon, and the last-mentioned died in the 37th year of the captivity of <margin>(*a*) 2 Kings 25:27.</margin> Jehoiachin, the King of Judah; and consequently, Jehoiachin was carried away into captivity in the year 150 of the Era of Nabonassar.

This capture occurred <margin>(*b*) 2 Kings 24:12.</margin> in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, and in the eleventh year of Jehoiakim’s reign: for the first year <margin>(*c*) Jeremiah 25:1.</margin> of Nebuchadnezzar corresponded with the fourth year of Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim <margin>(*d*) 2 Kings 23:36. 2 Chronicles 36:5.</margin> reigned eleven years before his deposition and the carrying away of his son Jehoiachin, and Jehoiachin himself reigned for three months, which ended with his captivity: so that the tenth year <margin>(*e*) Jeremiah 32:1.</margin> of Jehoiachin’s captivity corresponded with the 18th year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign. And the eleventh year of <margin>(*f*) Ibid. 52:5, 12.</margin> Zedekiah, in which Jerusalem was taken

From all this it is evident that Nebuchadnezzar began his reign in the year of Nabonassar 142—that is, two years before the death of his father Nabopolassar, who appointed him King during his own lifetime; that Jehoiakim <note>original: Jojakim</note> succeeded his father Josiah <note>original: Jofias</note> in the year of Nabonassar 139; and that Jerusalem was captured and the temple burned in the 160th year of that same era, approximately 20 years after Nineveh was destroyed.

According to the list of *Ptolemy*, the consensus of all chronologists, and several lunar eclipses, Darius Hystaspes <note>Darius I, known as Darius the Great, ruler of the Persian Empire.</note> began his reign over Persia in the spring of the year of Nabonassar 227. <margin>[g] Zechariah 7:1, 2, 3, 4, 5.</margin> "(g) And in the fourth year of King Darius, on the fourth day of the ninth month, called Chislev <note>original: Chisleu</note>, when they had sent Sharezer and Regem-Melech and his men to the house of God to entreat the favor of the Lord: saying to the priests who were in the house of the Lord of Hosts, and to the prophets: 'Must I weep in the fifth month, separating myself, as I have done for so many years?' Then the word of the Lord of Hosts came to Zechariah, saying: 'Speak to all the people of this land and to the priests, saying: "When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months for these seventy years, did you truly fast for me?"'" Calculate now these seventy years in which they fasted—in the fifth month for the burning of the temple, and in the seventh for the death of Gedaliah <note>Gedaliah was the governor of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem; his assassination is still commemorated by a fast day in the Jewish calendar.</note>—backwards from this time; so the burning of the temple and the death of Gedaliah will fall within the fifth and seventh Jewish months of the year of Nabonassar 160, as we stated above.

Just as the **Chaldean** astronomers counted the reigns of their Kings according to the years of Nabonassar, beginning each with the first day of the month **Thoth**, so the Jews counted theirs—according to the testimony of their writers—by the years of Moses, beginning each year with the month **Nisan**. If a king entered into his reign during that month, it was counted as a full year for him, and with the beginning of that month, the second year of his rule began. According to this calculation, the first year of Jehoiakim <note>original: Jojakim</note> began with the month of Nisan <note>The first month of the Hebrew ecclesiastical year, occurring in March–April.</note> of the year Nabon. 139 <note>Nabon. refers to the Era of Nabonassar, a chronological system starting in 747 BCE used by ancient astronomers like Ptolemy.</note>, although he perhaps only began his reign five or six months later. The fourth year of Jehoiakim, and the first year of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: Nebukadnezar</note>, began, according to the calculation of the Jews, with the month of Nisan of the year Nabon. 142. The first year of Zedekiah’s <note>original: Zedekiaas</note> reign, of Jehoiachin’s <note>original: Jojachins</note> captivity, and the ninth year of Nebuchadnezzar, began with the month of Nisan in the year Nabon. 150. And the tenth year of Zedekiah, and the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, began with the same month in the year Nabon. 159. Now, in the ninth year *(h)* of Zedekiah, Nebuchadnezzar fell upon Judea and its cities, and on the tenth day of the tenth month of that same year, he and his army besieged Jerusalem. And from this time until the tenth month of the second year of Darius there are exactly seventy years, with which the Prophet Zechariah <note>original: Zacharias</note> agrees, where he says: " *(i)* On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month (called *Shebat* <note>original: Schebath</note>) in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah. And then the Angel of the Lord answered and said: 'Lord of Hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which you have been indignant these seventy years?'" So it is that the ninth year of Zedekiah, in which God’s wrath against Jerusalem and the cities of Judah began, corresponds with the 158th year of Nabonassar, if that year is begun with the month of Nisan; and the eleventh year of Zedekiah, as well as the nineteenth of Nebuchadnezzar, in which Jerusalem was taken and the temple burned, falls within the year Nabon. 160, if it is begun with the same month, as we stated above.

From all these markers, the years of Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, and Nebuchadnezzar appear to be fully determined; and by this, the chronology of the Jews recorded in the Old Testament <note>original: Oude verbond; literally "Old Covenant."</note> is firmly linked <note>The Dutch catchword for the next page is "knogt," completing "verknogt" (linked/joined).</note> to the chronology of later centuries.

For between the death of Solomon <note>original: Salomon</note> and the ninth year of Zedekiah <note>original: Zedekias</note>, in which Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: Nebukadnezar</note> fell upon Judea and besieged Jerusalem, 390 years passed, as can be seen from the 4th chapter of Ezekiel <note>original: Ezechiel</note>, and from the years of the Kings of Judah when one totals them together. And from the beginning of Zedekiah's ninth year until the common Era or reckoning of Christ, 590 years have passed. If one now adds half of Solomon's reign <note>Solomon reigned for 40 years; half is 20 years.</note> to these two numbers, one will find exactly 1,000 years.

In the book of *Baruch (Ch. I. 2, 11 and 12)* one finds that Belshazzar <note>original: Belfazar</note>, in the fifth year of Jeconiah’s imprisonment, was the next in dignity to Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: Nebukadnezar</note> his father, and that the crown was intended for him, so that Evil-Merodach must have been in disgrace by then. Evil-Merodach ruled for two years after his father’s death, and was then, due to his wantonness and unrestraint, killed by Neriglissar <note>original: Nerigliffer</note> or Nergal-Sharezer, the husband of his sister, in the year 189 of the Era of Nabonassar, as *Ptolemy* <note>original: Ptolomeus</note> testifies.

Neriglissar reigned as guardian of his young son Labashi-Marduk <note>original: Labofordachus or Laboafferdach</note>, the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar through his daughter [the wife of Neriglissar], (*c*) for four years, including the short time that Labashi-Marduk ruled alone. For *Josephus* <note>original: Jofefus</note> and *Berossus* <note>original: Berofus</note> testify that Labashi-Marduk, after the death of his father, ruled for nine months, and that his friends then conspired with Nabonidus <note>original: Nabonnedus</note>, a Babylonian, and slew him at a feast because of his evil conduct; after which Nabonidus obtained the sovereignty by common consent: but these nine months are not specifically recorded in the list of *Ptolemy*.

Nabonidus or Nabonadius began his reign, according to *Ptolemy*, in the year 193 of the Era of Nabonassar, ruled for 17 years, and ended his reign in the year 210 of that Era, at which time Babylon was taken by Cyrus, and he was killed.

*Herodotus* <note>original: Herdoot</note> calls the last King of Babylon Labynetus, and says that he was the son of another Labynetus, and of Nitocris, an excellent Queen of Babylon.

By the first Labynetus, he <note>Likely referring to the historian Herodotus.</note> seems to mean a Prince of that name who, according to his account, ruled over Babylon when a great solar eclipse, which had been foretold by Thales, <note>Thales of Miletus, a Greek philosopher often credited with predicting the solar eclipse of 585 BCE, which ended a battle between the Medes and Lydians.</note> brought an end to the five-year war between the Medes and Lydians: and this Prince was the great Nebuchadnezzar. *Daniel (d)* calls the last King of Babylon Belshazzar, and says that Nebuchadnezzar was his father: and *Josephus (f)* <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> testifies that the last King of Babylon was called Naboandel by the Babylonians, and that he reigned 17 years. In my opinion, therefore, all these names belonged to the Belshazzar of *Daniel*, and this agrees better with the Holy Scriptures than the claim that Nabonidus was a Prince from outside the Royal house: for in Jeremiah (*Ch. xxvii:7*) it is said, "that all nations would serve Nebuchadnezzar, his son, and his son's son, until the time of his own land should come, when mighty nations and great Kings would make him serve them." Before the fifth year of Jehoiachin’s captivity, or the eleventh of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, Belshazzar was not only born but already held in esteem; and consequently, at the death of Evil-merodach, he was more than 34 years old, and could therefore be no other King than Nabonidus: for Laboafferdach, <note>Also known as Laborosoarchod, who reigned briefly as a child.</note> the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, was a child when he reigned.

*Herodotus (f)* relates that there had been two famous Queens of Babylon, named Semiramis and Nitocris; but that the latter was much wiser than the former. This Nitocris, observing that the Kingdom of the Medes had subdued many cities, and among them Nineveh, and had thereby become great and powerful, occupied the passes located between Media and Babylonia, and fortified them against any invasion. The river Euphrates, which ran in a straight <term>channel</term> <note>Dutch: "kil," referring to the bed or waterway of the river.</note>, she also diverted into many great bends, so that it would flow more gently and overflow less. From this it appears that the reign of Cyrus over Babylon began after the year Nabon. 208 and before the year Nabon. 211, and consequently in the years 209 or 210, which came between. In the year Nabon. 209, he arrived with his army before Babylon; *(m)* but that city defended itself bravely, and was only taken in the second year through the stratagem of Cyrus, who drained the Euphrates and climbed into the city from its empty channel <note>Cyrus diverted the river into a trench, allowing his troops to march into the city along the dry riverbed during a Babylonian festival.</note>. This certainly happened in late summer; for the snow, melting in the spring on the mountains of Armenia, caused the Euphrates to overflow at the beginning of summer, but by its middle, the water became low due to the heat. On the night that Babylon was conquered, Belshazzar *(n)* the King of the Chaldeans was also killed, and Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about 62 years old. This agrees with the list of *Ptolemy*, who says that Cyrus conquered Babylon in the year Nabon. 210, about one or two months after the summer solstice.

The Median Kings who ruled before Cyrus were Deioces, Phraortes, Astyages, Cyaxares, and Darius. The first three of these kings ruled before the monarchy of the Medes became powerful; but the last two made it great through their victories. For the poet *Aeschylus*, who flourished under the reigns of Darius Hystaspes and Xerxes, and died in the 76th Olympiad, introduces Darius lamenting over those who incited his son Xerxes to wage war against Greece, thus in *(o)*:

> That one man should rule all sheep-breeding Asia,
> Bearing the scepter of authority.

# OF THE BABYLONIANS AND MEDES

> <note>Original Greek: "Αλλ' ὁ ἐκείνȣ παῖς τόδ' ἔργον ἤνυσε· φρένες γὰρ αὐτȣ̃ θυμὸν ὠιακοστρόφȣν. Τρίτος δ' ἀπ' αὐτȣ̃ Κυ̃ρος εὐδαίμων ἀνὴρ, &c."</note> But his son completed this work; for his mind guided his spirit. And the third after him was Cyrus, a fortunate man, etc.

->That is<-

*They have performed a great work; for the falling city of Susa is destroyed: so great a work as never occurred since the time that King Jupiter granted this honor, that one man should rule over all fertile Asia, wielding a mighty scepter. For the first general was a Mede; he who followed him, and was his son, completed the work, because prudence guided his spirit; the third was Cyrus, a fortunate man, etc.* <note>The author is quoting Aeschylus’s tragedy *The Persians*. The "Mede" is generally identified as Cyaxares, his son as Astyages or Darius the Mede, and the third as Cyrus.</note>

The poet attributes here the founding of the Perso-Median monarchy to two Kings who ruled immediately before Cyrus, of whom the first was a Mede and the second was his son. This second one now was, according to <margin>[p] *Dan: VI. 1 & X. 1.*</margin> Daniel, Darius the Mede, whom Cyrus succeeded, and consequently the first was the father of Darius, that is Achsuerus, Assuerus, Oxyares, Axeres, the Prince Axeres or <term>Ky-Axeres</term><note>Cyaxares (reigned c. 625–585 BCE). The author suggests "Ky" is a title meaning "Prince," a common early linguistic theory.</note>, the word *Ky* signifying as much as Prince. For <margin>[q] *Dan. IX. 1.*</margin> Daniel tells us that Darius was a son of Achsuerus or Ahasuerus (as the <term>Masoretes</term><note>Jewish scholar-scribes who compiled the authoritative Hebrew and Aramaic text of the Old Testament.</note> incorrectly name him) from the seed of the Medes, that is, of the blood of the Median Kings. This is the <margin>[r] *Tob XVI. 17.*</margin> Ahasuerus who with Nebuchadnezzar took and destroyed Nineveh; which deed is attributed by the Greeks to Cyaxares, and by <margin>[s] *In Euseb. Praep. Euang. l. 9. c. 29.*</margin> Eupolemus <note>An early Jewish historian whose works survive only in fragments quoted by others.</note> to Astibares, a name that was perhaps incorrectly recorded for that of Ahasuerus. Through this victory over the Assyrians, through the overthrow of their monarchy which was established at Nineveh, and through the subsequent conquests of Armenia, Cappadocia, and Persia, this Ahasuerus laid the foundation for the rule of one man over all Asia; his son Darius completed that work through the capture of the kingdoms of Lydia and Babylon; and the third King was Cyrus, a fortunate man, as much for his many victories under and against Darius, as for his own extensive and peaceful reign.

<meta>This page continues the chronological investigation into the lineage of the Median and Persian kings. # OF THE ANTIQUITIES

Cyrus lived, according to *Cicero*, seventy years, and reigned, according to the list of *Ptolemy*, nine years over Babylon; consequently, he was 61 years old when he took that city, at which time (*t*) Darius the Mede was about 62 years of age. This Darius was therefore two generations younger than Astyages, the grandfather of Cyrus: for (*u*) *Herodotus* and (*v*) *Xenophon* <note>The author is comparing the two primary (and often conflicting) Greek sources for Persian history: Herodotus's *Histories* and Xenophon's *Cyropaedia*.</note> both testify that Astyages gave his daughter Mandane in marriage to Cambyses, a Prince of the Persians, and thereby became the grandfather of Cyrus. And, according to *Xenophon*, (*w*) Cyaxares was a son of Astyages and gave his own daughter to Cyrus as a bride. It was told, says (*x*) *Xenophon*, that this daughter of Cyaxares was very graceful, and that she was accustomed to play with Cyrus when they were both still children, and to say that she wanted to marry him, so that they must have been of approximately the same age. *Xenophon* further says that Cyrus married her after he had taken Babylon; but, since she would have been an old woman by then, it is more likely that he married her when she was still young and beautiful and he was in his youth. And this I consider to be the reason that Cyrus held command over the armies of Darius, his brother-in-law, until the time that he rose up against him. This then shows that Astyages, Cyaxares, and Darius reigned one after another in Media; and that Cyrus, who was a grandson of Astyages, married a sister of Darius and succeeded that Prince on the throne.

From this it appears that *Herodotus* has poorly described the chronology of the Kings Astyages and Cyaxares; for he (*y*) says that Cyaxares was the son and successor of Phraortes; the father and predecessor of Astyages, Mandane’s father; and the grandfather of Cyrus; whereby he claims that this Astyages took the daughter of Alyattes, King of Lydia, as his wife, and that he was finally captured by Cyrus and deposed from his dominion. And *Pausanias* followed Herodotus’s account where he relates that Astyages, the son of Cyaxares, reigned in Media in the days of Alyattes, the King of Lydia. It is true, Cyaxares had a son who [married] Ariene <note>Ariene was the daughter of Alyattes of Lydia, married to Astyages to seal a peace treaty after the Battle of the Eclipse (585 BCE).</note>

# OF THE ANTIQUITIES #

> " and destroy the King and the Princes thereof, says
> " the Lord. But it shall come to pass in the latter days [*na-*
> " *mely under Cyrus's reign*] <note>Cyrus the Great, who eventually liberated the Persians from Median rule and conquered Babylon.</note> that I will turn the captivity of
> " Elam, says the Lord."

The Persians were consequently until this time a free people, under their own King, but shortly thereafter they were warred upon, brought under, taken prisoner, and scattered among the nations that lay around them; and they persisted in their servitude until the time that Cyrus ascended the throne of Babylon. But because the Medes and Chaldeans did not attack the Persians until after the ninth year of Nebuchadnezzar, we obtain thereby the opportunity to investigate what the actions of the active military hero Cyaxares <note>King of Media (r. 625–585 BC) who helped destroy the Assyrian Empire.</note> were, immediately after he had overwhelmed Nineveh.

When Cyaxares drove the Scythians out of Media, some remained <gloss>(k)</gloss> in that land, who made their peace with him, and daily presented him with some venison that they brought down on the hunt. They, having caught nothing on a certain day, were threatened by Cyaxares, in his wrath, with insulting words. This treatment they took to heart, and shortly thereafter they killed a child of the Medes, prepared it as venison, presented it to Cyaxares, and then fled to Alyattes the King of Lydia; whereupon a war of five years followed between Cyaxares and Alyattes. From this history I conclude that the kingdoms of Media and Lydia at this time lay next to each other, and consequently that Cyaxares, shortly after the destruction of Nineveh, made himself master of the lands belonging to the Assyrian monarchy as far as the river Halys. In the sixth year of this war, on the 28th of May <gloss>(l)</gloss> of the year Nabon. <term>163</term> <note>The "Nabonassar Era," a chronological system starting in 747 BC; Year 163 corresponds to 585 BC.</note>, or 47 years before the conquest of Babylon by Cyrus, a great solar eclipse, which had been foretold by Thales <note>Thales of Miletus, the Greek philosopher often credited with the first prediction of a solar eclipse.</note>, caused a battle, which was being fought by the two Kings Cyaxares and Alyattes and was now at its fiercest, to cease entirely. Upon this, peace was established between those two Princes, through the mediation of Nebuchadnezzar the King of Babylon, and of Syennesis the King <note>Syennesis was the title or name of the Kings of Cilicia.</note>

These **Darics** <note>original: "Dariuſſen"; gold coins of the Persian Empire</note> were stamped on one side with an archer wearing a pointed crown, holding a bow in his right hand and an arrow in his left, and clothed in a long robe. I have seen one of these pieces in gold and one in silver: the first of which held the same weight and value as the Athenian **stater** <note>A standard silver or gold coin of the Greek world</note>, a gold piece that weighed two Athenian **drachmas**. It appears that Darius learned the art of minting money, and the use thereof, from the Lydians; and thereupon re-minted their gold: for before the conquest of Lydia, no money was in use among the Medes. *Herodotus* ($y$) recounts that when Croesus prepared himself for the war against Cyrus, a certain Lydian named Sandanis said to him, "that he was preparing for a campaign against a people clothed in leather trousers, who ate no food they desired but only what their barren land provided; who never drank wine but only water, and who did not sate themselves on figs or other good foods; who had nothing to lose, but could win much from the Lydians." For the Persians, says *Herodotus*, possessed no riches or anything of value before the conquest of Lydia. And *Isaiah* ($z$) says that the "Medes did not regard silver, and had no delight in gold." But the Lydians and Phrygians possessed such abundant riches that they even served as a proverb. *Pliny* says, ($a$) "Midas and Croesus had possessed infinite wealth. Already Cyrus, having conquered Asia, had found thirty-four thousand pounds [of gold], besides golden vessels and fashioned gold, and among it [golden] leaves and a plane tree and a vine. The extent of the Babylonian monarchy was roughly the same as that of Nineveh after the Medes had revolted from it. *Berosus* <note>A Babylonian priest and historian who wrote in Greek during the 3rd century BCE</note> says that Nebuchadnezzar ruled over Egypt, Syria, Phoenicia, and Arabia; and *Strabo* <note>An ancient Greek geographer and historian</note> adds Arbela <note>Modern-day Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan</note> to the territory of Babylon. This writer, stating that Babylon was the capital of Assyria, describes the boundaries of the Assyrian monarchy in this manner:

"Next to Persia and Susiana," (*h*) *he says*, "lies Assyria: for thus one calls Babylonia and the greater part of the region that extends around it: to this belongs Aturia, in which Ninus (or Nineveh) lies: it further includes Apolloniatis, the land of the Elymaeans and the Paraetaceni, Chalonitis by Mount Zagros, the plains situated near Ninus, Dolomene, Calachene, Chazene, Adiabene, the peoples of Mesopotamia near the Gordyaean mountains; and the Mygdones around Nisibis as far as Zeugma on the Euphrates; then a spacious region on this side of that river, which is inhabited by the Arabs and the Syrians (properly so called), and which extends to Cilicia, Phoenicia, Libya, the Sea of Egypt, and the Gulf of Issus." The same *Strabo*, setting down the extent of the province of Babylonia a little further on, says, "To the north, it is bounded by Armenia and Media as far as Mount Zagros."
