->### OF THE BABYLONIANS AND MEDES.<-

Darius was put to flight and taken prisoner by Cyrus; and through this victory, the monarchy of Asia passed over to the Persians. *Xenophon* calls the last King of the Medes *Cyaxares*, and *Herodotus* says that he was named *Astyages* and was the father of Mandane: but these Kings had already passed away before this time; and *Daniel* the prophet has left us the correct name of the Median King, just as the *Darics* <note>original: "Darius-sen"; these are gold coins famously associated with the Persian monarchs, which the author uses as evidence for the King's name</note>, which were minted by that last Prince, also demonstrate that his name was *Darius*. From *Herodotus* <margin>[u] Book 1, chapter 127, etc.</margin> however, we learn that he was defeated by Cyrus in the manner previously related.

It was about two years after the conquest of Babylon when Cyrus achieved this victory over Darius. For the reign of Nabonnedus, the last King of the Chaldeans—who is called Naboandel and Belshazzar by *Josephus*—ended, according to *Ptolemy’s* list, in the year of Nabonasser 210, and nine years before the death of Cyrus; but after the transfer of the empire of the Medes to the Persians, Cyrus reigned alone for seven years, as *Xenophon* <margin>[v] Cyropaedia, Book 8, page 233.</margin> testifies. This Prince spent the seven winter months annually in Babylon, the three spring months in Susa, and the two summer months in Ecbatana; and when he came to Persia for the seventh time, he died there and was buried at Pasargadae. According to the list of *Ptolemy*, and the consensus of all chronologists, he died in the year of Nabonasser 219; consequently, he defeated Darius in the year of Nabonasser 212, and 72 years after the destruction of Nineveh. He defeated his army for the first time in the year of Nabonasser 211, after he had rebelled against him in the same year, or at the end of the preceding one, and declared himself King of Persia. Cyrus was, according to *Herodotus*, seventy years old when he died, and consequently, he was born in the year of Nabonasser 149, of his mother Mandane, who was a sister of Cyaxares (then a youth) and of Amytis, the wife of Nebuchadnezzar: and his father Cambyses descended from the ancient Royal house of the Persians.

# CHAPTER V.

->*Description of Solomon’s Temple.*<-

<margin>See plates I and II</margin>The Temple of Solomon having been destroyed by the Babylonians, it will not be out of place to provide a description of that structure here.

The Temple stood in the west [a] on a square courtyard, called the separate place <note>original: "afgezonderde plaats"; this refers to the *Gizrah*, an area of the Temple complex mentioned in Ezekiel</note>: in front of it stood the altar [b] in the center of another square courtyard, called the inner court, or the Court of the Priests; and these two squares, which were separated from each other only by a row of marble railings, formed a plain from east to west 200 cubits <term>cubit: an ancient unit of measure based on the length of the forearm, roughly 18 to 21 inches</term> long, and from south to north 100 cubits wide. This rectangular square was enclosed on the west side by a wall, and on the other three sides by a pavement 50 cubits wide, [c] upon which stood buildings for the Priests, with galleries beneath them; and the pavement was decorated on the inner side with marble railings in front of the galleries: this entire area from west to east was thus 250 cubits long and 200 cubits wide, and was enclosed on the outside by a courtyard, called the great court, or the Court of the People, [d] which was 100 cubits wide on each side; for Solomon built no more than two courts. The outer court lay about four cubits lower than the inner one; it was surrounded on the west side by a wall, and on the other three sides by a pavement fifty cubits wide, [e] upon which stood buildings for the people. This entire space was called the Sanctuary [f] and occupied a square 500 cubits long and 500 cubits wide: it was surrounded by a walkway 50 cubits wide, which was called the mountain of the house <note>The Temple Mount, known in Hebrew as *Har HaBayit*</note>; this walkway was enclosed with a wall, six cubits high and wide, and 600 cubits long on each side. The cubit was twenty-one and a half

### OF SOLOMON'S TEMPLE.

Dd

...or nearly 22 inches by the English foot \*, this being the holy cubit <term>holy cubit: a measurement used for sacred structures, approximately 21.8 inches, distinct from the shorter "common" cubit</term> of the Jews, which was one handbreadth, or a sixth part, longer than the common cubit.

The altar stood in the center of the entire structure; and between the buildings of both courts (*g*), opposite the middle of the altar, to the east, south, and north, were gates, 25 cubits wide between the buildings (*h*), and 40 cubits long; besides portals of another 10 cubits, which faced the inner court; so that the entire length of the gates or entrances, across the pavement, was 50 cubits. <margin>Plate III.</margin> Each gate had two doors, one on each side, 10 cubits wide and 20 cubits high, with posts and sills 6 cubits wide: within the gates, between the sills, was a space 28 cubits long and 13 cubits wide; and on each side of this space were three posts, each 6 cubits square and 20 cubits high, between which were vaults 5 cubits wide: these posts and vaults together filled the length of 28 cubits between the sills; and their width, when added to the 13 cubits of the space, made up the total width of the entrances, or 25 cubits. The posts were hollow and contained within them small chambers with little windows for the gatekeepers; in front of each of these chambers was a step one cubit wide. The walls <margin>Plate I.</margin> of the gates, which were 6 cubits thick, were also hollow and contained rooms within them serving various purposes. At the eastern gate of the court of the people, called the King’s Gate (*i*), there were six gatekeepers, and at the southern and northern gates there were four each: the people entered and (*k*) exited through the southern and northern gates; but the eastern gate was opened only for the King (*l*), and there he ate his sacrificial offerings. On each floor there were in total (*r*) 30 chambers, in which the people ate the sacrifices; or otherwise thirty high sections, each containing three chambers—a lower, a middle, and an upper chamber. Each section was 37 and a half cubits long and was supported by four pillars in each row, whose foundations or bases were 4 and a half cubits square. The space between the bases occupied 6 and a half cubits, and the distance between the center-points of the pillars was eleven cubits: and where two sections joined, the bases of the pillars stood against each other, so that the space between the centers of these two pillars occupied only 4 and a half cubits. At the front, this gap was filled with a marble column 4 and a half cubits square, beyond which half of the pillars projected on either side; an arrangement possibly ordained for the strengthening of the building. At the ends of these buildings, in the four (*s*) corners of the court of the people, were small square courts that measured 50 cubits on the outside of the wall and 40 cubits on the inside of the wall on each side: these courts served for the placement of stairs to climb to the buildings, and for kitchens to roast and boil the meat of the sacrifices for the benefit of the people; each kitchen was 30 cubits wide and each staircase 10 cubits wide. The buildings of the court of the priests <note>the inner court reserved for the clergy</note> were 37 and a half cubits long between each gate, and contained on each floor one large chamber, which was further divided into smaller rooms for the use of both the high officials of the temple and the Princes of the priests. OF THE ANTIQUITIES

# VI. CHAPTER.

->*Of the Antiquities of the Persians.*<-

Cyrus, having transferred the sovereignty to the Persians and ruled for seven years, was succeeded by his son Cambyses, who reigned for seven years and five months, and in the last three years of his reign subjected Egypt to his rule. He was followed by Mardus, or Smerdis the Magus, who passed himself off as Smerdis, the brother of Cambyses.

Smerdis ruled for seven months, and in the eighth month he was discovered and slain along with a large number of the Magi—a name the Persians gave to their priests; and in memory of this day, the Persians celebrated an annual festival which they called "the day of the slaughter of the Magi." After this, Marasus and Artaphernes ruled for a few days, and then Darius, the son of Hystaspes and grandson of Arsamenes, of the lineage of Achaemenes, a Persian, ascended the throne, being chosen as King by the neighing of his horse <note>According to the historian Herodotus, several noblemen agreed that whoever’s horse neighed first at sunrise would be king. Darius’s groom used a clever trick to ensure his horse neighed first.</note>: before his reign he bore the name Ochus <margin>[a] Valerius Maximus, book 9, chapter 2.</margin> (*a*). It appears that on this occasion he reformed the order of the Magi, and appointed his father Hystaspes as Chief or Archimagus <term>Archimagus: a title meaning "High Priest" or head of the Magi</term> of the same; for Porphyrius tells us <margin>[b] Porphyry, On Abstinence, book 4.</margin> (*b*), "that the Magi were a class of people held in such venerable esteem that Darius, the son of Hystaspes, wrote upon the monument in honor of his father, among other things, that he had been Chief of the Magi." ### OF THE PERSIANS.
<sig>Ee 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: To</meta>

> “...performed: but, having gradually increased, they have
> “ grown to the name and greatness of a complete nation:
> “ and inhabiting villages, which are not fortified by walls,

This monarchy was then, in its beginning, composed of various nations, each of which had until now retained its own religion: but now *Hystaspes* and *Zoroaster* collected from all of these that which they judged best, gave to it the authority of laws, and taught their institutions to others; and these in turn taught others, until the number of their disciples was large enough to perform the Priesthood through the whole monarchy: in place of the old and diverse religious practices that were maintained in various regions, these two men introduced their religion throughout the entire Persian empire, in nearly the same manner as Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of Rome's religious and political institutions</note> designed and established the religion of the Romans. This new Persian religion was partly derived from the institutions of the Chaldeans <note>An ancient people of Mesopotamia famous for their astrology and wisdom</note>, in which Zoroaster was well-versed, and partly from the teachings of the Brahmans <note>Ancient Indian priests and philosophers</note>, by whom Hystaspes had been instructed: there are those who suppose that the latter [the Brahmans] derived their name from the Abrahamites, or the sons of the Patriarch Abraham, born of his second wife Keturah <note>According to Genesis, Keturah's sons were sent by Abraham to the "East country"</note>; that they were instructed by their father in the service of ONE GOD, without images, and sent toward the East; and that they thus passed this religion down to Hystaspes. Around the same time as Hystaspes and Zoroaster lived *Ostanes*, another excellent Magus: *Pliny* places him under Darius Hystaspes, and *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world</note> makes him the follower of Zoroaster: he came with Xerxes into Greece and seems to be the Otanes of Herodotus, who discovered the false Smerdis <note>A pretender who briefly usurped the Persian throne; Otanes is credited with exposing the fraud because the man lacked ears</note>, and planned the conspiracy against him, for which service he was held in honor by the conspirators, and remained free from obedience to Darius.

In the sacred explanation of the customs of the Persians, these words are attributed to Zoroaster: <margin>(a) Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 1, final chapter.</margin> *(a)* “God has the head of a hawk; he is the first...” <note>original Greek: Ὁ Θεὸς ἔστι κεφαλὴν ἔχων ἱέρακος· οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ πρῶτος</note>

And the same is taught by Ostanes <note>An ancient Persian magus and alchemist often cited in Hellenistic literature</note>, in his book called *Octateuchus*. This was the God of the Persian Magi, and they served him by keeping an everlasting fire burning on an altar (which stood in the middle of a circle or round plain, and which circle was surrounded by a trench) for the lighting of sacrifices, without using any temples, or worshipping deceased men and images. But in a short time they fell away from the service of this eternal and invisible God to the worship of the sun, fire, deceased men, and images, just as the Egyptians, Phoenicians, and Chaldeans had done before. Because of these superstitions, and some alleged prophecies, the words *Magi* and *Magia* <note>The root of our modern word "magic"</note>, which first signified the priests and the religion of the Persians, were subsequently used in a bad sense.

Darius or Darah <note>Darius I, also known as Darius the Great</note> began his reign in the spring of the sixteenth year of the Persian monarchy, or the year of Nabonassar 327 <note>The "Era of Nabonassar" was a chronological system used by ancient astronomers; 327 is likely a transcription error for 227 (c. 521 BCE)</note>, and reigned 36 years, as all chronologists agree. In the second year of his reign, the Jews, through the encouragement of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, began to build the temple, and completed it in his sixth year. In the year of Nabonassar 258 <note>c. 490 BCE</note> he fought against the Greeks at Marathon, ten years before the battle of Salamis, and in the fifth year thereafter he died, at the end of winter or the beginning of spring, in the year of Nabonassar 263 <note>c. 485 BCE</note>. To Darius the Mede they attribute one or at most two years (*Daniel 9:1*). To Cyrus three incomplete years (*Daniel 10:1*); to Ahasuerus twelve years before the casting of the lot (*Esther 3:7*), one year between that time and the dominance of the Jews over their enemies (*Esther 9:1*), and one more year until the time when Esther and Mordecai wrote the second letter to keep the feast of Purim <note>The Jewish festival commemorating the salvation of the Jewish people from Haman's plot</note> (*Esther 9:29*), and thus in total 14 years. And to Darius the Persian they give 32 or rather 36 years (*Nehemiah 13:6*). So that according to this calculation, the monarchy of the Persians, from the second year of Darius Hystaspes, in which the temple was built, until its subjection by Alexander the Great, flourished for no longer than 32 years: and thus the Jews calculate in their great chronicle called *Seder Olam Rabbah* <note>term: Seder Olam Rabbah; a 2nd-century CE Hebrew language chronology of biblical history from the creation to the revolt of Bar Kokhba</note>. This latter Darius, who is Darius Nothus <note>Darius II, reigned 423–404 BCE</note>, he considers to be the same Darius who was conquered by Alexander the Great <note>Actually Darius III; Josephus's chronology famously compresses the Persian period</note>, and according to this calculation, he makes Sanballat and Jaddua the high priest still to be alive when Alexander overthrew the Persian monarchy. All the Jews thus conclude the list of Persian Kings with Artaxerxes Longimanus <note>original: "Langhand," meaning "Long-hand"</note> and Darius Nothus, and recognize no other Kings of Persia than those recorded in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. On this basis, they hold Artaxerxes Longimanus, Artaxerxes Mnemon, and Artaxerxes Ochus to be but one single King:

-># CONCERNING ANTIQUITIES<-

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

...Darius Nothus and Darius Codomanus <note>Darius Nothus reigned 423–404 BCE; Darius Codomanus was the last king of Persia, reigned 336–330 BCE</note> as a single Darius; and the high priests Jaddua and Simon the Just as one and the same person. And everything they find in secular writings concerning Artaxerxes Mnemon, Artaxerxes Ochus, and Darius Codomanus, they attribute to the Artaxerxes and Darius mentioned in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. Those Jews who regarded Herod as the Messiah, and for that reason bore the name of Herodians, seem to have based that opinion on the 70 weeks of years <note>A prophecy from Daniel 9:24–27 used to calculate the time until the Messiah's arrival; a "week of years" is 7 years</note> which they found had elapsed between the reigns of Cyrus and Herod. But when they later applied that prophecy to Theudas, Judas the Galilean, and finally to Bar Kokhba <note>Leaders of Jewish revolts against Rome between 6 CE and 135 CE</note>, it appears they shortened the years of the Persian Empire. Since their accounts in this matter are very imperfect, it was necessary for us to seek recourse in the writings of the Greeks and Romans, and in the list of Ptolemy <note><term>Ptolemy's Canon</term>: A chronological list of kings and their reign lengths, used by ancient astronomers to date celestial events</note>, to reconstruct the chronology of this monarchy. This being done, we have a better foundation to clarify and settle the Jewish history recorded in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah; for this history, having been obscured by the passage of time, requires some clarification. To begin here, I will first set down in order the history of the Jews under Zerubbabel, during the reigns of Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius Hystaspes.

This history is contained partly in the book of *Ezra*, from its beginning to the sixth verse of the fourth chapter, and partly in that of *Nehemiah* from *Chapter VII:5* to *Chapter XII:9*. For *Nehemiah* copied this part of his book from the chronicles of the Jews that had already been written before his day: as can be seen both from reading that passage and from the observation that the priests and Levites who sealed the covenant on the 24th day of the seventh month (*Nehemiah 10*) were the same as those who returned to Judea in the first year of Cyrus (*Nehemiah 12*). And that all those who returned also sealed it can be seen from the following comparison of their names.

Thus the Darius who, in the book of *Ezra*, is named before and after Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes, and the Darius who follows in the same book, are, according to the book of *Esdras*, one and the same Darius. Cyrus and Ahasuerus <note>original: "Ahasueros"</note> being placed [before] Darius Hystaspes; it follows that the Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes <note>original: "Arthahshashta"</note> who follow him are Xerxes and Artaxerxes Longimanus <note>Artaxerxes I, nicknamed "Long-hand"</note>; and the Jews, who came from Artaxerxes to Jerusalem, and began to build the city with *(b)* its wall, were Ezra and his companions. After the temple was completed and Darius Hystaspes had died, the enemies of the Jews, at the beginning of the reign of King *(c)* Ahasuerus or Xerxes, who had succeeded Darius, wrote an accusation against them; but in the seventh year of his successor Artaxerxes, *(d)* Ezra, along with his companions, traveled from Babylon to Jerusalem with *(e)* offerings and the *(f)* vessels for the temple, and with orders to withdraw from the King’s *(g)* treasury whatever they deemed necessary for the service of God's house; and for this reason it is said (*Ezra VI. 14.*) that the temple was finished according to the command of Cyrus <note>original: "Cores"</note>, Darius, and Artaxerxes <note>original: "Arthahshashta"</note> the King of Persia. The commission of Ezra further gave him power to appoint *(h)* governors and judges in Judea; and this people thereby becoming a new political body, a great council or Sanhedrim <term>Sanhedrim: the supreme judicial and administrative council of the Jews</term> was called together to separate the people from their foreign wives, by which council they were also encouraged to build Jerusalem and its wall, and for this reason *Ezra* says in his *(i)* prayer: "that God had extended mercy to them in the sight of the Kings of Persia, and given them a little reviving to set up the house of their God, and to repair the desolations thereof, and to give them a garden <note>The Dutch "tuin" (garden) here refers to a "fence" or "hedge" in the biblical sense of a protected enclosure; modern English Bibles usually translate this as "wall".</note>, or wall in Judah and in Jerusalem." But when they had now begun to restore the wall, their enemies wrote against them to Artaxerxes. "Be it known *(k)* unto the King," they say, "that the Jews, who came up from you—"

He, arriving in Jerusalem in that same year, remained there as *(q)* governor for 12 years and built the wall: and being opposed in this work by *(r)* Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem, <note>Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arab were local leaders who opposed the restoration of Jerusalem's defenses.</note> he nevertheless persevered with great steadfastness and patience until all the gaps in the wall were repaired. Sanballat *(s)* and Geshem, hearing this, sent messenger after messenger to him to prevent him from setting the doors in the gates; but he nevertheless remained steadfast in the work until the doors were hung. And thus the wall was completed in the 28th *(t)* year of Artaxerxes, on the *(u)* 25th of the month of Elul, <term>Elul: the sixth month of the Hebrew ecclesiastical calendar, usually coinciding with parts of August and September</term> or the sixth month, in fifty-two days after the gaps had been repaired and work had begun on the gates. For while the timber for the doors was being hewn and prepared, they worked on the gaps in the wall; and both these matters required time and are therefore not to be counted together within the 52 days. These days indicate the time in which the final work on the wall was performed—the work of erecting the doors—after the timber had been prepared and the gaps had been closed. marched westward, subjected all of Syria and Judea to himself, and took and destroyed the city of Jerusalem. It seems that they <note>The "they" refers to Eastern or Persian historians whose accounts the author is critiquing.</note> call Nebuchadnezzar a general of Lohorasp, because he assisted that king in some of his wars. The fifth king of this dynasty they call Kishtasp, and by this name they sometimes mean Darius the Mede, and at other times Darius Hystaspes. For they say that he was a contemporary of Ozair <note>The Arabic/Persian name for the biblical prophet Ezra.</note> or Ezra, and of Zaradust or Zoroaster, the lawgiver of the Ghebers or fire-worshippers, and that he introduced their teachings throughout all of Persia, and thus he would be Darius Hystaspes. But they also say that he lived at the same time as Jeremiah and Daniel, and that he was the son and successor of Lohorasp, and consequently Darius the Mede. The sixth king of the Kaianids bears the name of Bahaman among them, and this Bahaman was, because of the great extent of his dominion, according to their saying, also called *Ardfchir Diraz*, that is, Artaxerxes Longhand <note>Originally *Artaxerxes Langhand*, referring to Artaxerxes I (Longimanus), so named because his right hand was reportedly longer than his left.</note>. And yet they say that Bahaman marched westward toward Mesopotamia and Syria, defeated Belshazzar the son of Nebuchadnezzar, and granted that kingdom to Cyrus, his Lieutenant General over Media; and according to this account, Bahaman must have been Darius the Mede. Next after Ardfchir Diraz they place a certain Queen Homai, the mother of Darius Nothus, although she did not actually rule. And the two following, and last kings of the Kaianids, they call Darab the illegitimate son of Ardfchir Diraz, and Darab who was defeated by Askander Roumi; that is Darius Nothus, and the Darius who was pushed from the throne by the Greek Alexander <note>The author refers to Darius III, the last king of the Achaemenid Empire, defeated by Alexander the Great.</note>. But the kings who reigned between these two Dariuses, they skip over, as well as Cyrus, Cambyses, and Xerxes. From their stories, however, it appears that the dynasty of the Kaianids was that of the Medes and Persians, which began with the revolt of the Medes from the Assyrians, at the end of Sennacherib's reign, and ended with the conquest of Persia by Alexander the Great. But their history of this dynasty is very incomplete, as some kings are skipped therein, and others are confused with one another: and the chronology thereof is even worse; for to the first king they give a reign of 120 years, to the second one of 150 years,

<meta>This page concludes the author's comparison of Eastern and Western chronologies, specifically focusing on how various nations inflated the reign lengths and antiquity of their early kings to appear more ancient and venerable.</meta>

<page-num>247</page-num>
->### OF THE PERSIANS.<-

...to the third [reign] one of 60 years, to the fourth and fifth each one of 120 years, and to the seventh one of 112 years.

This dynasty, corresponding now with the monarchies of the Medes and Persians, must mean that the Pishdadians <note>The Pishdadian dynasty is the first dynasty of Persian mythology, described in the *Shahnameh*. The author is attempting to reconcile these legendary figures with historical Assyrian rulers.</note>, who immediately preceded them, were the Assyrians. And according to Eastern histories, this was the oldest kingdom in the world; some of its kings lived for an uncommonly long time, with one ruling for 500, another 700, and a third for 1,000 years.

We need not wonder then that the Egyptians made the kings of the first dynasty of their monarchy—who reigned in Thebes during the days of David, Solomon, and Rehoboam—so uncommonly old and long-lived; since the Persians did the same with their kings, who began to reign in Assyria two hundred years after the death of Solomon; and the Syrians likewise with their kings Adar <note>Likely referring to Ben-Hadad, a common name for Aramean/Syrian kings in the Bible.</note> and Hazael, who ruled a good hundred years after Solomon, "honoring them as gods and boasting of their antiquity, not knowing," *as Josephus says*, <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD) was a Roman-Jewish historian. This reference is likely to his work *Antiquities of the Jews*, where he discusses the Syrian kings.</note> "that they were only of recent origin."

And since these peoples have so excessively exaggerated their antiquities, we need not be surprised that the Greeks and Latins <note>The early inhabitants of central Italy and the founders of Rome.</note> placed their first kings a little earlier than they actually were.

<summary>This page argues that ancient civilizations, including the Persians, Egyptians, and Syrians, significantly exaggerated the reigns and antiquity of their early kings to gain prestige. The author uses this to justify a more skeptical approach to the early chronologies of the Greeks and Romans.</summary>
<keywords>chronology, Pishdadian dynasty, Assyrians, Egyptian kings, King Solomon, Hazael, Josephus, historical exaggeration, ancient monarchies</keywords>

# CORRECTIONS. <note>Original: "Verbeteringen"</note>

Page <note>Original: "B.", abbreviation for "Bladzijde"</note> 4, line <note>Original: "r.", abbreviation for "regel"</note> 23, read <note>Original: "l.", abbreviation for "lees"</note> for *established*, *described*. Page 15, line 14, read 58. Page 27, line 3 from the bottom, read 747. Page 35. line 3, read for 26, 29. Page 43, last line <note>Original: "r. ultima", using Latin "ultima" for last</note> read for *all*, *still*. Page 56, line 16, read 58. Page 70. line 27. read *reign of Cranaus* <note>Cranaus was a legendary king of Athens.</note>. Page 86, line 27, read 35 *years*. Page 152, line 8, read 34*th*. Page 152, line 29, read 30 *years*. Page 166, the note, line 1 read *Chron.* <note>Original: "Kron.", abbreviation for "Kronieken" (Chronicles)</note>. Page 186. the note. line 1 & 3, read 2 *Kings XXIV*. <note>Original: "Kon.", abbreviation for "Koningen" (Kings)</note>.

# EXPLANATION
### OF THE
### ADJACENT PLATE.

**ABCD.** The designated place upon which the Temple stood.
**EFGH.** The Court of the Gentiles. <note>The outermost area of the Temple complex where non-Jews were permitted to enter.</note>
**I.** The *Susa* Gate. <note>original: "Poort Susa"; the eastern gate of the Temple, named after the Persian capital to commemorate the return from exile.</note>
**PHRYGICED.** A pavement, encompassing the three rows of the Courts of the Israelites, upon which the buildings for the Priests and Levites were located.
**MNOP.** The Court of the Women.
**NOTSRN.** The Court of the Israelites, or the foremost Court, in which the people presented themselves with solemn faces. <note>original: "met gelaten ende zich, hielden"; referring to the area where Jewish men gathered for prayer and sacrifice.</note>
**VXYZ.** The Court of the Priests.
**1.** The Altar of burnt offerings.
**2.** The Brazen Sea. <note>original: "koperen Zee"; a massive bronze basin used by priests for ritual purification.</note>
**3.** The copper stands. <note>original: "koperen Hand-vaten"; likely referring to the wheeled bases or supports for the portable lavers.</note>
**4.** The ten copper basins. <note>The smaller lavers used for washing the parts of the sacrifices.</note>
**5.** The ascent to the Court of the People, or the King's Gate, located in the middle of the southern Court.
**6.** The chambers above the gates of the Court of the People, in which the Councils of the Jews <note>The Sanhedrin or local judicial bodies.</note> sat on each floor.
**7.** The Court of the Temple, or the place for rest and walking.
**8.** The ascent from the Court of the Gentiles, to which the steps of the Court of the People climbed.
**9.** The steps of the Court of the People, in which there were three doors.

<meta>The text on this page provides a detailed legend for the architectural floor plan illustrated in the accompanying plate. It specifically describes the layout of the inner court and the priestly quarters of a temple, likely based on the biblical descriptions in the Book of Ezekiel or the Temple of Solomon.</meta>

# EXPLANATION
### OF THE
## ADJACENT PLATE.

**ABCD.** The separate place <note>original: *afgezonderde plaats*, referring to the restricted area of the temple sanctuary</note>.
**ABEF.** The Inner Court, or Court of the Priests, of the separate place, and the pavement on the three other sides, separated by a row of marble railings.
**G.** The Altar.
**HHH.** The east, south, and north gates of the Court of the Priests.
**IIIIII.** The galleries supporting the buildings for the Priests.
**KK.** Two courts or squares, in which were staircases and kitchens of the priests.
**L.** Ten steps ascending to the porch <note>original: *portaal*, likely the vestibule or *Ulam*</note> of the Temple.
**M.** The Porch of the Temple.
**N.** The Holy Place or the Sanctuary <term>Sanctuary: In this context, the *Hekhal* or the main hall of the temple</term>.
**O.** The Holy of Holies <term>Holy of Holies: The innermost chamber of the temple, the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, where the presence of God was said to dwell</term>.
**PPPP.** Thirty treasuries <note>original: *schatkamers*</note> standing in two rows, opening door to door into a middle gallery, and surrounding the three sides of the Sanctuary and the Holy of Holies.
**Q.** The winding staircase to the middle chamber above the Sanctuary.
**RRRRRR.** The buildings for the 24 priestly orders, standing on the pavement on both sides of the separate place. These were three stories high, without galleries on the ground level; but the rooms of the upper stories were narrower than those of the lower, as galleries ran in front of them. On each floor were 24 rooms, 12 on each side, which opened into a passage or gallery **SS** which stretched along the length between the buildings.
**TT.** Two squares or courts, in which were kitchens for the Priests of the 24 orders <note>The 24 orders refer to the divisions of priests established for service in the Temple</note>.
